about: A shared UK-wide revision pack, not one university's syllabus, used alongside population health, evidence-based practice, medical sociology, statistics, ethics and law, and communication teaching at several UK medical schools from Year 1 through the clinical years. It covers the GMC Medical Licensing Assessment areas 'Social and population health' and 'Medical ethics and law': study design, measures of risk, screening, statistics, health inequalities, ethical frameworks, the law on consent, capacity and confidentiality in England and Wales, and professional communication. Law and guidance points are dated and should be checked against the current source. Educational material only, not legal or clinical advice.

notes.h: Epidemiological study designs: choosing and critiquing them
notes.overview: Epidemiology asks who gets disease, when, where and why. Each study design answers a different question, and each has typical weaknesses. To read a paper well, work out how the participants were sampled, what was measured and when, and then how chance, bias and confounding could explain the result.
objectives: Distinguish descriptive, observational analytical and experimental designs by how participants are sampled.
Explain why a case-control study gives an odds ratio and a cohort study gives risks and rates.
Distinguish bias from confounding and name ways to control each.
Apply Bradford Hill's viewpoints to judge whether an association is likely to be causal.
Choose a suitable design for a given research question and justify the choice.

sections.body:
Designs are usually grouped as descriptive (case reports, case series, ecological and cross-sectional studies), observational analytical (case-control and cohort studies) and experimental (randomised controlled trials). Systematic reviews then combine studies.
- Ecological study: compares groups or areas, not individuals, for example national salt intake against stroke mortality. It is cheap and generates hypotheses, but risks the ecological fallacy (assuming that a group-level link holds for individuals).
- Cross-sectional study: measures exposure and outcome in a population at one point in time. It gives prevalence, but because both are measured together it usually cannot show which came first.
- Case-control study: people are selected by outcome (cases with the disease, controls without) and their past exposures are compared.
- Cohort study: people are selected by exposure and followed over time (prospectively, or using historical records) to compare how often the outcome occurs.
- Randomised controlled trial (RCT): the investigator allocates the intervention at random and compares outcomes.
- Systematic review and meta-analysis: a reproducible search and appraisal of all relevant studies, sometimes with statistical pooling.

sections.h: Why designs differ: sampling, chance, bias and confounding
sections.body:
The sampling decides which measure you can calculate. In a cohort, the denominators are people at risk, so risks (or rates per person-time) and a relative risk follow. In a case-control study the investigator fixes how many cases and controls there are, so risks cannot be estimated; you compare the odds of exposure in cases and controls, giving an odds ratio.
Any observed association may reflect:
- Chance: random variation, addressed by sample size, confidence intervals and p-values.
- Bias: systematic error. Selection bias arises from who enters or stays in the study; information bias from how exposure or outcome is measured (for example recall bias, when cases remember exposures differently from controls, and observer bias).
- Confounding: a third factor associated with the exposure, independently associated with the outcome and not on the causal pathway. Smoking confounds an apparent link between alcohol and lung cancer.
Confounding can be controlled at the design stage (randomisation, restriction, matching) or in the analysis (stratification, multivariable models, standardisation). Randomisation is the only method that also balances confounders nobody has measured.

- Case-control: efficient for rare diseases and long latency (for example Doll and Hill's 1950 smoking and lung cancer study); vulnerable to recall bias and to poor choice of controls.
- Cohort: shows that exposure came before outcome and can study several outcomes of one exposure (for example the British Doctors Study from 1951); slow, costly, and biased if loss to follow-up is related to exposure or outcome.
- RCT: the strongest design for testing treatments; allocation concealment, blinding and intention-to-treat analysis protect it, but it can be expensive, short and unrepresentative, and it is unethical for harmful exposures.
Bradford Hill (1965) proposed nine viewpoints for judging causation: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient (dose-response), plausibility, coherence, experiment and analogy. They are aids to judgement, not a checklist. Temporality (the exposure must come before the outcome) is the one generally regarded as essential.

A structured appraisal asks:
- What was the question? Frame it as population, intervention or exposure, comparison and outcome (PICO).
- Is the design suitable for that question? Treatments are best tested in RCTs; harms and rare outcomes often need case-control or cohort data.
- For a trial: was allocation random and concealed, were participants and assessors blinded, were the groups similar at baseline, was follow-up complete, and was the analysis by intention to treat (analysing people in the groups they were randomised to)?
- For an observational study: how were participants selected, how were exposure and outcome measured, and which confounders were adjusted for?
- How large and how precise is the effect (confidence interval), and does it apply to your patients?
Reporting guidelines help readers check that the key information is present. Trials are reported against CONSORT; the CONSORT 2025 update has a 30-item checklist plus a participant flow diagram.

A paediatric team wonders whether a rare childhood cancer is linked to living near high-voltage power lines. A cohort study would need to follow millions of children for years to collect enough cases. A case-control study is the efficient choice: take cases from a cancer registry, pick population controls of similar age from the same source population, and compare how many lived near power lines.
The team should then anticipate the weaknesses. Address records are better than parents' memories, because recall can differ between cases and controls. Controls must come from the population that produced the cases, or selection bias will distort the comparison. Social deprivation might be associated with both housing near power lines and the outcome, so it is a possible confounder to adjust for. Even a statistically significant odds ratio would then be judged against Bradford Hill's viewpoints, especially temporality, dose-response and consistency with other studies, before anyone calls it causal.

- Students often call any study using past data a case-control study. In fact the defining feature is sampling: a case-control study selects by outcome, whereas a retrospective (historical) cohort selects by exposure using old records.
- Students often think randomisation removes all bias. It balances confounders at baseline, but poor allocation concealment, lack of blinding or differential drop-out can still bias a trial.
- Students often treat an adjusted association as proof of causation. Adjustment only handles confounders that were measured, and measured well, so residual confounding remains.
- Students often think a cross-sectional study can show cause and effect. Because exposure and outcome are measured at the same time, it usually cannot show which came first.

notes.h: Measures of disease frequency and association
notes.overview: Frequency measures (prevalence, incidence) describe how much disease there is. Association measures (risk ratio, odds ratio, risk difference) compare groups. Trial measures (absolute and relative risk reduction, number needed to treat) turn results into decisions for patients. Most exam marks come from building the 2×2 table correctly and choosing the right measure for the design.
objectives: Distinguish prevalence, incidence proportion and incidence rate, and explain how duration links incidence to prevalence.
Calculate a risk ratio, odds ratio, risk difference and attributable fractions from a 2×2 table.
Explain why the odds ratio approximates the risk ratio only when the outcome is rare.
Calculate ARR, RRR and NNT, and explain why relative effects alone can mislead patients.
Interpret a standardised mortality ratio.

sections.body:
- Prevalence = people with the disease ÷ population, at a point in time (point prevalence) or over a period (period prevalence). It is used to plan services.
- Incidence proportion (cumulative incidence, or risk) = new cases over a period ÷ people at risk at the start.
- Incidence rate = new cases ÷ total person-time at risk. Example: 24 new cases over 4,000 person-years is 6 per 1,000 person-years.
- In a stable population with low prevalence, prevalence ≈ incidence rate × average duration. A treatment that prolongs life without curing (for example antiretroviral therapy for HIV) raises prevalence even if incidence does not change; a quick cure or rapid death lowers it.
Comparing crude rates between populations with different age structures misleads. Direct standardisation applies each population's age-specific rates to one standard population. Indirect standardisation applies standard age-specific rates to the study population to get the expected number of deaths, giving the standardised mortality ratio: SMR = observed ÷ expected × 100. If a town has 120 deaths when 80 were expected, its SMR is 150 (50% more deaths than expected for its age structure).

sections.h: The 2×2 table and measures of association
sections.body:
Lay the table out with exposure in rows and outcome in columns: a = exposed with outcome, b = exposed without, c = unexposed with outcome, d = unexposed without.
- Risk ratio (relative risk, RR) = [a/(a+b)] ÷ [c/(c+d)]. Used in cohort studies and trials.
- Odds ratio (OR) = (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = ad/bc. The only valid ratio in a case-control study, because the investigator fixes how many cases and controls there are. When the outcome is rare, b ≈ a + b and d ≈ c + d, so the OR approximates the RR; when the outcome is common, the OR lies further from 1 than the RR.
- Risk difference (attributable risk) = risk in exposed − risk in unexposed.
- Attributable fraction in the exposed = (RR − 1) ÷ RR: the share of cases among exposed people that the exposure explains, if causal.
- Population attributable fraction (Levin's formula) = Pe(RR − 1) ÷ [1 + Pe(RR − 1)], where Pe is the proportion of the population exposed: the share of all cases that would be avoided if the exposure were removed.
A ratio of 1 (or a difference of 0) means no association. A 95% confidence interval for a ratio that includes 1 is compatible with no effect at the 5% level.

sections.h: Trial measures: ARR, RRR and NNT
sections.body:
From a trial with a control event rate (CER) and experimental event rate (EER):
- Absolute risk reduction (ARR) = CER − EER.
- Relative risk reduction (RRR) = ARR ÷ CER (equivalently 1 − RR).
- Number needed to treat (NNT) = 1 ÷ ARR, rounded up, and always stated with its time frame and outcome. For harms, the same calculation gives the number needed to harm (NNH).
Worked example: stroke over 5 years in 20% on placebo and 15% on treatment. ARR = 5 percentage points, RRR = 25%, NNT = 1/0.05 = 20 over 5 years.
Because NNT depends on baseline risk, the same RRR gives very different NNTs. If a lower-risk patient's 5-year stroke risk is 2%, a 25% RRR reduces it to 1.5%: ARR 0.5 percentage points and NNT 200. This is why shared decision-making uses absolute figures.

In a cohort, 30 of 1,000 smokers and 20 of 2,000 non-smokers develop disease X.
- Risks: 30/1,000 = 3% in smokers; 20/2,000 = 1% in non-smokers. RR = 3.
- Risk difference = 2 percentage points, so NNH = 1/0.02 = 50 over the study period.
- Attributable fraction in smokers = (3 − 1)/3 ≈ 67%.
- Pe = 1,000/3,000 = 1/3. PAF = (1/3 × 2) ÷ (1 + 2/3) = 0.67 ÷ 1.67 = 0.4.
- Check by another route: overall risk = 50/3,000 ≈ 1.67%; (1.67 − 1)/1.67 ≈ 0.4. So, if causal, 40% of all cases in this population are due to smoking.

Measuring frequency
- Prevalence = people with the disease ÷ population, at a point in time (point prevalence) or over a period (period prevalence). It is used to plan services.

Lay the table out with exposure in rows and outcome in columns: a = exposed with outcome, b = exposed without, c = unexposed with outcome, d = unexposed without.

notes.h: Screening: principles, test performance and pitfalls
notes.overview: Screening means offering a test to people without symptoms to find those at higher risk, so that earlier action reduces harm. Whether a programme does more good than harm depends on the condition, the test, the treatment and the programme as a whole. Predictive values depend on prevalence, and several biases make screening look better than it is.
objectives: Distinguish screening from case-finding and diagnostic testing.
Calculate sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV and likelihood ratios from a 2×2 table.
Explain why PPV falls as prevalence falls, using natural frequencies.
Explain lead-time bias, length-time bias and overdiagnosis, and why RCT mortality is the right outcome.
Apply the Wilson and Jungner and UK NSC criteria to a proposed programme.

sections.h: What screening is, and the classic criteria
sections.body:
Screening is the systematic offer of a test to people who do not have symptoms, to identify those at higher risk of a condition so that further tests or early treatment can reduce harm. It differs from diagnostic testing (people with symptoms) and from case-finding (opportunistically testing people already in contact with services).
Wilson and Jungner (WHO, 1968) set out the classic principles:
- the condition should be an important health problem, with a recognisable latent or early stage and a natural history that is adequately understood
- there should be a suitable, acceptable test, and facilities for diagnosis and treatment
- there should be an accepted treatment and an agreed policy on whom to treat
- the cost of case-finding should be balanced against spending on medical care as a whole, and case-finding should be a continuing process.

sections.h: Test performance and why predictive values depend on prevalence
sections.body:
From a 2×2 table of test result against true disease status (TP, FP, FN, TN):
- Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN): the proportion of people with the disease who test positive.
- Specificity = TN/(TN + FP): the proportion of people without it who test negative.
- Positive predictive value (PPV) = TP/(TP + FP); negative predictive value (NPV) = TN/(TN + FN).
- Likelihood ratio positive = sensitivity/(1 − specificity); likelihood ratio negative = (1 − sensitivity)/specificity.
Sensitivity, specificity and likelihood ratios are properties of the test. PPV and NPV also depend on prevalence: when a disease is rare, even a small false-positive rate applied to the large number of healthy people produces more false positives than true positives.
Worked example (10,000 people, prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90%, specificity 95%): 100 have the disease (TP 90, FN 10) and 9,900 do not (TN 9,405, FP 495). PPV = 90/585 ≈ 15.4%; NPV = 9,405/9,415 ≈ 99.9%. At 10% prevalence the same test gives TP 900, FP 450 and PPV = 900/1,350 ≈ 66.7%.

- Lead-time bias: diagnosis is moved earlier, so survival measured from diagnosis looks longer even if the person dies at the same time.
- Length-time bias: slow-growing disease spends longer in the detectable pre-symptomatic phase, so screening finds a higher share of indolent, better-prognosis cases.
- Overdiagnosis: screening finds disease that would never have caused symptoms or death in the person's lifetime, leading to treatment and its harms without benefit.
- Healthy volunteer (selection) bias: people who choose to attend tend to be healthier than those who do not.
For these reasons the convincing evidence is a randomised trial showing lower disease-specific (and ideally overall) mortality or morbidity in the group offered screening, not longer survival from diagnosis. The UK NSC criteria also require that the benefits outweigh harms such as overdiagnosis and false positives, which is why informed choice matters.

sections.h: UK screening policy (guidance; check for updates)
sections.body:
The UK National Screening Committee (UK NSC) advises ministers and the NHS in all four UK nations. Its criteria (updated 2022) cover the condition, the test, the intervention, the programme and implementation. Key expectations are high-quality randomised trial evidence that screening reduces mortality or morbidity, benefits that outweigh harms such as overdiagnosis and false positives, value for money, and information that allows people to make an informed choice.
Recent decisions illustrate this:
- Cervical screening in England moved to HPV primary testing, and from July 2025 people aged 25 to 49 who test HPV negative are invited every five years rather than three.
- Prostate cancer: in May 2026 the UK NSC recommended against screening all men or Black men as a group, and recommended targeted two-yearly PSA testing for men aged 45 to 61 with a BRCA2 variant and a relevant family history. The government accepted this for England, with rollout expected from 2027; the devolved nations decide separately.
Screening intervals and eligible groups change, so check the UK NSC and NHS programme pages for current details.

A company offers a blood test for pancreatic cancer to healthy 50-year-olds, quoting 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity. In this group prevalence is perhaps 1 in 1,000. Out of 100,000 people tested, about 100 have the cancer and 90 test positive; of the 99,900 without it, 5% (4,995) also test positive. Roughly 5,085 people get a positive result, and only about 1 in 57 of them actually has cancer (PPV ≈ 1.8%).
Every false positive leads to anxiety, imaging and possibly biopsy, each with its own risks. Ten cancers are missed and those people may be falsely reassured. There is no randomised evidence that detecting pancreatic cancer this way lowers mortality. Against the UK NSC criteria the test fails several requirements, even though its sensitivity and specificity sound impressive. The same test may be far more useful in a symptomatic or very high-risk group, where prevalence and so PPV are higher.

- Students often assume a sensitive test has a high PPV. PPV depends heavily on prevalence and specificity, so it can be low even for a good test in a low-risk population.
- Students often judge screening by survival from diagnosis. Lead-time and length-time bias inflate survival; use mortality in randomised trials.
- Students often think 'early detection can only help'. Overdiagnosis, false positives, false reassurance and complications of follow-up tests are real harms.
- Students often treat maximum uptake as the aim. UK programmes aim for informed choice, so people who decline after understanding the trade-offs are making a valid decision.
- Students often confuse sensitivity with PPV. Sensitivity starts from people with the disease; PPV starts from people with a positive test.

notes.h: Statistics for medicine: inference, tests and interpretation
notes.overview: Statistics lets you judge how far a sample result reflects the population and how much is chance. The essentials are matching the summary and test to the type of data, reading confidence intervals before p-values, and separating statistical significance from clinical importance.
objectives: Distinguish standard deviation from standard error, and calculate a 95% confidence interval for a mean.
Interpret a p-value and a confidence interval correctly, including a non-significant result.
Explain type I and type II errors, power, and the problem of multiple testing.
Choose an appropriate test for a given type of data and study design.
Interpret correlation, regression and survival analysis outputs at an introductory level.

sections.h: Types of data and how to summarise them
sections.body:
Data are categorical (nominal, such as blood group; or ordinal, such as cancer stage) or numerical (discrete counts, or continuous measurements such as blood pressure). The type decides the summary, the graph and the test.
- Roughly symmetrical (normal) numerical data: mean and standard deviation (SD).
- Skewed numerical data (for example length of hospital stay): median and interquartile range.
- Categorical data: counts and percentages.
For normally distributed data about 68% of values lie within 1 SD of the mean and about 95% within 1.96 SD. Reference ranges in laboratories are often built this way, which is why roughly 1 in 20 healthy people falls outside a 'normal range'.

sections.h: Standard error, confidence intervals and p-values
sections.body:
The SD describes how spread out individual values are. The standard error of the mean (SE = SD/√n) describes how precisely the sample mean estimates the population mean; it shrinks as the sample grows.
A 95% confidence interval (CI) for a mean is approximately mean ± 1.96 × SE. Example: mean systolic BP 140 mmHg, SD 12, n = 36. SE = 12/6 = 2, so the 95% CI is 140 ± 3.92, about 136.1 to 143.9 mmHg. If the study were repeated many times, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean. Quadrupling n to 144 halves the SE (to 1) and halves the width.
The p-value is the probability of getting a result at least as extreme as the one observed if the null hypothesis (no difference) were true. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about the size of the effect. For a difference the null value is 0; for a ratio it is 1. A 95% CI that excludes the null value corresponds to p < 0.05.

- Type I error (false positive): rejecting a true null hypothesis. Its probability, α, is conventionally set at 0.05.
- Type II error (false negative): failing to detect a real effect. Its probability is β; power = 1 − β, usually planned at 80–90%.
- Power increases with larger sample size, larger true effect and higher α, and falls with more variable data. Many small trials are underpowered, so 'no significant difference' often means 'not enough evidence' rather than 'no effect'. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
- Multiple testing: with 20 independent tests at α = 0.05, about one 'significant' result is expected by chance alone. The Bonferroni method divides α by the number of tests (five tests: significant only if p < 0.01); it is conservative when tests are correlated.
- Subgroup analyses should be pre-specified, few in number and tested for interaction; otherwise they are hypothesis-generating.

Ask: what type is the outcome, how many groups are there, and are the observations paired?
- Two independent groups, normal continuous outcome: unpaired (two-sample) t-test; skewed data: Mann–Whitney U test.
- Paired measurements (before and after in the same people): paired t-test; skewed data: Wilcoxon signed-rank test.
- More than two groups: one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA); non-parametric: Kruskal–Wallis test.
- Proportions in independent groups: chi-squared test; Fisher's exact test when expected counts are small. Paired proportions: McNemar's test.
- Association between two continuous variables: Pearson's correlation coefficient r (linear, normal data) or Spearman's rank correlation.
- Predicting an outcome while adjusting for other variables: linear regression (continuous outcome), logistic regression (binary outcome, giving adjusted odds ratios) or Cox proportional hazards regression (time-to-event outcome, giving hazard ratios), with Kaplan–Meier curves and the log-rank test to compare survival.

A trial of a new antihypertensive in 200 people reports that systolic BP fell 2 mmHg more than placebo (95% CI 0.5 to 3.5 mmHg, p = 0.01). The result is statistically significant, but a 2 mmHg difference may be too small to matter clinically, and the interval shows the true effect is at most about 3.5 mmHg.
A second, smaller trial of a different drug reports a 10 mmHg greater fall (95% CI −2 to 22 mmHg, p = 0.10). It is not statistically significant, but the interval includes large and clinically important benefits; the trial was probably underpowered. The correct conclusion is 'uncertain, needs a larger trial', not 'the drug does not work'.
Reading the CI and asking what difference would change practice (the minimum clinically important difference) avoids both errors.

- Students often confuse SD with SE. SD describes the spread of individual values; SE describes the precision of an estimate and shrinks with larger samples.
- Students often read p = 0.03 as 'a 97% chance the treatment works'. The p-value is calculated assuming no true effect; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true.
- Students often treat p = 0.06 as proof of no effect. Look at the confidence interval and the study's power.
- Students often use t-tests on skewed data or on proportions. Use non-parametric tests for skewed data and chi-squared (or Fisher's) for proportions.
- Students often treat correlation as causation, or read r as the slope. r measures the strength of a linear relationship; the regression slope gives the change in outcome per unit change in the predictor.

notes.h: Health inequalities: patterns, explanations and responses
notes.overview: Health inequalities are systematic, avoidable and unfair differences in health between groups. In the UK, health follows a social gradient: it gets worse at each step down the social ladder, not only at the bottom. To answer well, you need the evidence, the competing explanations and the policy responses, and you need to show that behaviours are themselves socially patterned.
objectives: Distinguish health inequality from health inequity, and explain the social gradient.
Explain the four explanations in the Black Report and evaluate them.
Describe the Dahlgren and Whitehead model, the inverse care law and proportionate universalism.
Apply Core20PLUS5 and the Equality Act 2010 to a local service problem.
Evaluate how individually focused interventions can widen inequalities.

sections.body:
A health inequality is any measurable difference in health between groups. Health inequity refers to differences that are systematic, avoidable and unjust. Differences can be by socioeconomic position (income, education, occupation, area deprivation), ethnicity, sex, geography, disability, or membership of inclusion health groups (for example people experiencing homelessness, people in contact with the justice system, Gypsy, Roma and Traveller communities).
The social gradient means health gets steadily worse at each step down the socioeconomic scale. The Whitehall studies of British civil servants showed mortality and coronary heart disease rising with each step down the employment grades, among people who were all in stable office jobs, and this was only partly explained by smoking and other conventional risk factors.
The Marmot Review 10 Years On (2020) reported that improvement in life expectancy in England had stalled, inequalities had widened, and life expectancy had fallen for women in the most deprived 10% of areas.

The Black Report (1980) set out four explanations:
- Artefact: the gradient is a product of how class and health are measured. Largely rejected, because the gradient persists across many measures.
- Natural or social selection: ill health causes people to move down the social scale. It explains some of the gradient but not most of it.
- Cultural or behavioural: groups differ in smoking, diet, alcohol and exercise. These matter, but behaviours are shaped by circumstances.
- Materialist or structural: income, housing, work, education and environment directly shape health. The Report favoured this explanation.
Later work adds psychosocial pathways (control at work, chronic stress) and a life-course view, in which disadvantage accumulates from early childhood. notes.h: Medical ethics: frameworks and core debates
notes.overview: Ethics gives the reasons behind clinical choices. The law sets a minimum and GMC guidance sets professional standards, but neither settles every question. Strong answers name the conflict, look at it through more than one framework, weigh the competing considerations and reach a conclusion they can defend.
objectives: Explain the four principles and why they are prima facie rather than absolute.
Distinguish consequentialist, deontological and virtue-based reasoning, and apply each to a case.
Apply the doctrine of double effect and the acts and omissions distinction to end-of-life care.
Evaluate QALY-based resource allocation and procedural fairness ('accountability for reasonableness').
Distinguish what is legal from what is ethical in a given dilemma.

sections.body:
- Four principles (Beauchamp and Childress, from 1979): respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. Gillon (1994) stressed that each is prima facie (binding unless it conflicts with another) and added attention to scope: to whom, and how far, each duty applies.
- Consequentialism (Bentham, Mill): the right act produces the best overall outcome. Act utilitarianism judges each act; rule utilitarianism follows rules whose general observance produces the best outcomes. The main criticism is that it can justify sacrificing individuals for aggregate benefit.
- Deontology (Kant): some duties bind regardless of outcome, and people must never be treated merely as a means. It underpins consent, truth-telling and confidentiality.
- Virtue ethics (Aristotle): ask what a practically wise, compassionate and honest doctor would do. Related approaches include care ethics (relationships and dependency) and casuistry (reasoning from paradigm cases).

sections.h: How to reason through a dilemma
sections.body:
A reliable structure:
- Identify the facts, including what is uncertain, and who is affected.
- Name the conflict, for example autonomy against beneficence, or the individual against the population.
- Apply more than one framework and see whether they converge.
- Check the law (statute and case law) and GMC guidance; law usually sets the minimum, while ethics asks what is best.
- Reach a reasoned conclusion, acknowledge the strongest counter-argument, and say what would change your view.
Two tools recur in end-of-life questions:
- The doctrine of double effect: an act with a foreseen bad effect may be permissible if the act itself is good or neutral, only the good effect is intended, the bad effect is not the means to the good, and there is proportionate reason. It is often invoked when giving symptom relief that might, as a side effect, shorten life.
- Acts and omissions: in Airedale NHS Trust v Bland (1993) the courts held that stopping artificial nutrition in good faith, when continuing is no longer in the patient's best interests, allows the existing condition to take its course and is lawful, whereas positive action to cause death (as in the prosecution of Dr Cox) is unlawful.

- Autonomy against beneficence: a capacitous adult may refuse any treatment, even if life-saving (Re T 1992; Ms B v An NHS Hospital Trust 2002). Overriding a refusal normally needs a finding that the person lacks capacity.
- Truth-telling: withholding information is rarely justified; Montgomery (2015) keeps the 'therapeutic exception' narrow.
- Justice and resources: NICE uses cost per quality-adjusted life year (QALY). Critics argue QALYs can disadvantage older and disabled people, and the 'rule of rescue' pulls towards identifiable patients. Daniels and Sabin's 'accountability for reasonableness' asks that rationing decisions be public, based on relevant reasons, open to appeal and revision, and enforced. Courts will not themselves decide how limited budgets are allocated (R v Cambridge Health Authority, ex parte B, 1995).
- Conscientious objection: the Abortion Act 1967 (s4) allows objection to participating in treatment, interpreted narrowly as hands-on participation rather than administrative or supervisory tasks (Greater Glasgow Health Board v Doogan, 2014); patients must still be able to access care.

sections.h: Current law and policy points (guidance; check for updates)
sections.body:
- Assisted dying in England and Wales: assisting or encouraging suicide is an offence under s2 Suicide Act 1961, and actively ending a patient's life is murder. In R (Nicklinson) v Ministry of Justice (2014) the Supreme Court declined to declare s2 incompatible with Article 8, and several Justices said Parliament was the right forum.
- The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill passed the Commons in June 2025 but fell at the end of the session in spring 2026 when Lords committee stage ran out of time. A new private member's bill with the same title was introduced in the 2026-27 session and was defeated at Commons second reading on 11 September 2026 (286 to 270). The law is therefore unchanged, but check for further bills.
- NICE cost-effectiveness: from April 2026 the standard threshold for technology appraisals rose from £20,000–£30,000 to £25,000–£35,000 per QALY.

A man newly diagnosed with HIV refuses to let you tell his wife, who is not aware of the risk. Respect for his autonomy and confidentiality conflicts with non-maleficence towards an identifiable person at serious risk. A deontologist stresses the duty of confidence and the trust it sustains; a rule utilitarian notes that a general rule of confidentiality encourages people to test and disclose, but also that preventing serious harm to an identifiable person can justify an exception. A virtuous doctor would work hard to persuade him, explain the risk to his wife and offer support with partner notification.
If persuasion fails, GMC confidentiality guidance allows disclosure without consent in the public interest to protect a person from a risk of death or serious harm, after telling the patient what you intend to do where it is safe to do so, and recording your reasoning. The frameworks converge on 'persuade first; disclose as a proportionate last resort'.

notes.h: Law: consent, capacity and confidentiality (England and Wales)
notes.overview: Valid consent needs capacity, enough information and a voluntary choice. When an adult lacks capacity for a decision, the Mental Capacity Act 2005 decides who acts and on what basis. Confidentiality is a legal and professional duty, and it has defined exceptions. The law here is for England and Wales; Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own statutes.
objectives: Explain the elements of valid consent and the Montgomery test for disclosing risks and alternatives.
Apply the MCA 2005 principles and the two-stage capacity test in the order set out in JB (2021).
Apply the best-interests checklist and identify who can lawfully decide for an adult without capacity.
Distinguish Gillick competence, the Fraser guidelines and s8 Family Law Reform Act 1969.
Decide when confidential information may be disclosed without consent, using GMC guidance.

sections.body:
Valid consent needs capacity, adequate information and voluntariness (no undue influence: Re T, 1992).
- If a patient has agreed to the broad nature of a procedure, a claim in battery fails (Chatterton v Gerson, 1981); inadequate information about risks is dealt with in negligence.
- Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11: doctors must take reasonable care to ensure the patient knows of any material risks of the recommended treatment and of reasonable alternatives. A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to it, or if the doctor knows or should reasonably know that this particular patient would. This needs dialogue, and the 'therapeutic exception' is narrow.
- McCulloch v Forth Valley Health Board [2023] UKSC 26: which alternatives count as 'reasonable' is decided by the professional practice test (Bolam in England and Wales); the doctor must then explain those alternatives.
- A capacitous adult may refuse any treatment, even life-saving (Re T, 1992; Ms B, 2002).

sections.h: Capacity under the Mental Capacity Act 2005
sections.body:
The MCA applies to people aged 16 and over. Its five principles (s1): assume capacity unless it is established that the person lacks it; take all practicable steps to help the person decide; an unwise decision does not by itself show incapacity; act in the person's best interests; and consider the less restrictive option.
Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. Following A Local Authority v JB [2021] UKSC 52, ask first the functional question: is the person unable to understand the relevant information, retain it, use or weigh it, or communicate the decision (s3)? Only then ask whether that inability is caused by an impairment of, or disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain (s2).
- Information must be explained in a way that suits the person; brief retention can be enough.
- Relevant information includes the foreseeable consequences of deciding either way, or not deciding.

sections.h: Deciding for adults who lack capacity, and children
sections.body:
- Best interests (s4): consider whether the person may regain capacity, involve them, and weigh their past and present wishes and feelings, beliefs and values, and the views of carers, family and any attorney. It is not substituted judgement, but it is assessed from the patient's point of view and covers welfare in the widest sense (Aintree v James, 2013).
- 'Next of kin' has no legal power to consent for an adult. A health and welfare attorney (LPA) or court-appointed deputy can decide within their authority; otherwise the clinician proposing treatment decides in best interests.
- A valid and applicable advance decision to refuse treatment (made at 18 or over, with capacity) binds clinicians. If it refuses life-sustaining treatment it must be in writing, signed, witnessed and include a statement that it applies even if life is at risk.
- Disagreements that cannot be resolved locally can be taken to the Court of Protection.
- Children: 16 and 17-year-olds can consent under s8 Family Law Reform Act 1969. Under-16s can consent if Gillick competent, with the Fraser guidelines applying to contraception.

sections.h: Confidentiality and deprivation of liberty (guidance; check for updates)
sections.body:
GMC confidentiality guidance (2017, updated 2018 for data protection law) allows disclosure:
- with consent (implied consent covers sharing within the team for direct care);
- when required by law (for example a court order);
- in the public interest, chiefly to protect people from a risk of death or serious harm (W v Egdell, 1990). Where safe, tell the patient first, disclose the minimum and record your reasons; do not ask for consent to a disclosure you have already decided to make.
Driving: the driver must tell the DVLA. If an unfit patient keeps driving, persuade them, tell them you will disclose, inform the DVLA medical adviser, then confirm in writing.
ABC v St George's (2020) accepted that, in a close relationship, clinicians may owe a relative a duty to balance genetic risk information against confidentiality.
Deprivation of liberty: in June 2026 the Supreme Court replaced the Cheshire West 'acid test' with a multifactorial assessment, in which a person lacking capacity may give or withhold valid consent through their wishes and feelings. The Liberty Protection Safeguards have not been implemented.

She cannot retain the key facts long enough to weigh them, and this inability is caused by her dementia, so she lacks capacity for this decision. Her son has no legal authority without an LPA. The team decides in her best interests: her wish to go home and her current objection count, as do the likely benefits of surgery (pain relief, the best chance of walking again and returning home) and the anaesthetic risks. A best-interests meeting with family and a geriatrician is wise, and continued disagreement goes to the Court of Protection.

notes.overview: Professionalism means being accountable for patient safety and trust. It is more than good manners. This topic covers the GMC's standards, consultation and bad-news structures, candour when things go wrong, raising concerns, and how doctors are held to account. Medical students are expected to meet equivalent standards.
objectives: Explain the structure and domains of Good medical practice (2024) and how it applies to students.
Apply the Calgary-Cambridge guide and a stepwise approach to breaking bad news.
Distinguish the statutory (organisational) and professional (individual) duties of candour.
Apply the duty to raise concerns about a colleague or system, including escalation routes.
Explain the legal test for gross negligence manslaughter and what the Bawa-Garba appeal decided.

Good medical practice (GMC) sets the standards for doctors. The 2024 edition came into effect on 30 January 2024. It has four domains, all equally important: knowledge, skills and development; patients, partnership and communication; colleagues, culture and safety; and trust and professionalism.
The 2024 edition gives more emphasis to respectful, fair and supportive workplaces. For the first time it says explicitly that doctors must not act in a sexual way towards colleagues that causes offence, embarrassment, humiliation or distress, and that doctors who witness bullying, harassment or discrimination should support the person affected and challenge or report the behaviour where appropriate. It also stresses speaking up about errors and concerns.
The GMC's guidance for medical students mirrors these standards, and medical schools use it in student fitness to practise processes.

The Calgary-Cambridge guide breaks a consultation into five tasks: initiating the session, gathering information, building the relationship, giving information (explaining and planning), and closing the session. In the expanded version of the guide, physical examination sits between gathering information and explanation, and providing structure (signposting and summarising) and building the relationship run through the whole consultation.
Useful skills: open-to-closed questioning; exploring ideas, concerns and expectations (ICE); 'chunk and check'; teach-back; and shared decision-making using absolute risks and natural frequencies, including the option of doing nothing. Use a professional interpreter rather than family members, and never a child.
Breaking bad news follows a predictable sequence, often taught with the SPIKES mnemonic (Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy and summary, developed by Buckman and Baile):
- prepare: read the notes, choose a private space, offer a companion, avoid interruptions
- find out what the patient already knows or suspects, and how much they want to know
- give a warning shot, then the news in clear, jargon-free chunks
- pause and allow silence; acknowledge and respond to emotion with empathy
- check understanding, agree a plan, summarise, safety-net and arrange follow-up.

- Statutory duty of candour: Regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 applies to CQC-registered organisations. After a notifiable safety incident they must tell the person in person as soon as reasonably practicable, give an account of the facts, apologise, offer support, follow up in writing and keep records.
- Professional duty of candour (joint GMC and NMC guidance): every individual clinician must tell the patient (or those close to them) when something has gone wrong, apologise, offer a remedy or support, explain the short- and long-term effects, and be open with colleagues, employers and regulators.
- An apology does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence (s2 Compensation Act 2006).
- Raising concerns: doctors must act promptly when patient safety or dignity may be seriously compromised, whether by a colleague's conduct, health or performance or by systems and resources. Escalate through supervisor, consultant or clinical director, then the medical director, and then the regulator if needed. The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers who make protected disclosures.

sections.h: Accountability (law and regulation; check for updates)
sections.body:
- Fitness to practise: the GMC investigates concerns, and Medical Practitioners Tribunal Service (MPTS) tribunals decide whether a doctor's fitness to practise is impaired and what sanction applies (for example conditions, suspension or erasure).
- Gross negligence manslaughter (R v Adomako, House of Lords, 1994): the defendant owed a duty of care, breached it, the breach caused death, and the breach was so gross that it deserves criminal punishment, judged on all the circumstances.
- Bawa-Garba v GMC [2018] EWCA Civ 1879: after a doctor's conviction for gross negligence manslaughter, the tribunal suspended her; the High Court substituted erasure at the GMC's request. The Court of Appeal restored the suspension, holding that appeal courts should be slow to interfere with a specialist tribunal's evaluative judgment, and that the tribunal could take account of systemic failings and other people's responsibility. The case prompted reviews of how gross negligence manslaughter applies in health care and how reflection is used.

On a night shift an FY1 prescribes a penicillin-class antibiotic to a 70-year-old man, missing a documented penicillin allergy. He develops a rash and wheeze after the first dose, is treated promptly and recovers fully. A nurse suggests there is 'no need to make a fuss as he's fine'.
The professional duty of candour still applies: the patient should be told what happened, receive an apology and an explanation of any possible effects, and have the allergy re-documented. The FY1 should inform the supervising consultant, complete an incident report so that the system (allergy alerts, prescribing checks) can learn, and reflect on the event. Whether the trust's statutory duty is triggered depends on the level of harm, which the organisation decides. An apology is the right thing to do and is not of itself an admission of negligence. Concealing the error would be a far more serious professional failing than the error itself.

- Students often treat professionalism as etiquette. It is about accountability, patient safety and public trust, enforced through fitness to practise.
- Students often confuse statutory and professional candour. Statutory candour is an organisational duty triggered by notifiable incidents; professional candour applies to every clinician whenever something goes wrong.
- Students often fail to escalate because the colleague is senior. Seniority does not change the duty to protect patients.
- Students often believe an apology admits liability. Section 2 of the Compensation Act 2006 says it does not of itself.
- Students often use a relative or child to interpret. Professional interpreters protect accuracy, confidentiality and the relative's role.

cards.f: What defines a case-control study?
cards.b: Participants are selected by outcome (cases with the disease, controls without), and their past exposures are compared, usually as an odds ratio.
cards.ex: Sampling on outcome is the key: ask 'were people chosen because they had the disease?'

cards.f: Retrospective cohort vs case-control study
cards.b: A retrospective cohort selects people by exposure from historical records and looks forward in record-time to outcomes; a case-control study selects by outcome and looks back at exposure.
cards.ex: Both use past data, so timing does not separate them; the sampling variable does.

cards.f: Why can't you calculate a relative risk from a case-control study?
cards.b: The investigator fixes the numbers of cases and controls, so the proportion with disease in each exposure group is set by design, not by nature; only the odds ratio is valid.
cards.ex: Risk needs a denominator of people at risk; case-control sampling destroys it.

cards.f: How does randomisation deal with confounding?
cards.b: Chance allocation makes the arms similar on average in every characteristic, measured or unmeasured, so a later difference in outcomes is attributable to the intervention or to chance.
cards.ex: Adjustment can only handle measured confounders; randomisation balances unknown ones too.

cards.f: Three criteria for a confounder
cards.b: Associated with the exposure; independently associated with the outcome; not on the causal pathway between exposure and outcome.
cards.ex: If it lies on the pathway (exposure → factor → outcome) it is a mediator, and adjusting for it hides a real effect.

cards.f: Bias vs confounding
cards.b: Bias is systematic error in how participants are selected or data measured; confounding is a real third factor mixing its effect with the exposure's. Confounding can be adjusted for in analysis if measured; most bias cannot.
cards.ex: Ask: is the error in the method (bias) or in the world (a third variable)?

cards.f: A case-control study of birth defects finds mothers of affected babies report more medicine use in pregnancy. What bias should you suspect?
cards.b: Recall bias: mothers of affected babies are likely to search their memories harder than control mothers. Prescription records would reduce it.
cards.ex: Recall bias is the classic weakness of case-control designs that rely on memory.

cards.f: Countries with higher average chocolate consumption win more Nobel prizes per head. Can you conclude that chocolate-eaters are more likely to win?
cards.b: No. This is the ecological fallacy: a group-level correlation need not hold for individuals, and national wealth may confound it.
cards.ex: Ecological data describe areas, not people.

cards.f: Why is temporality the one Bradford Hill viewpoint regarded as essential?
cards.b: A cause must come before its effect. Without temporality the association could be reverse causation; the other viewpoints only strengthen or weaken the case.
cards.ex: Strength, gradient or plausibility can all be absent for a true cause, but the order in time cannot be.

cards.f: An RCT analyses only participants who completed treatment. What problem does this create?
cards.b: A per-protocol analysis breaks randomisation: people who stop treatment often differ (sicker, more side effects), so the comparison can exaggerate benefit. Intention-to-treat analysis avoids this.
cards.ex: Keep people in the arm they were randomised to.

cards.f: Which design for: does a common drug cause a rare adverse effect that appears years later?
cards.b: Usually a case-control study (or a large cohort built from routine records): an RCT would be too small and too short to capture a rare, late harm.
cards.ex: Rare and late outcomes favour sampling on outcome.

cards.f: Odds ratio from a 2×2 table
cards.b: OR = ad/bc: odds of the outcome (or exposure) in one group divided by the odds in the other.
cards.ex: Cross-multiply the diagonal cells.

cards.f: Why does the odds ratio approximate the risk ratio only for rare outcomes?
cards.b: When the outcome is rare, the number with the outcome is tiny compared with the number without, so odds (a/b) ≈ risk (a/(a+b)). With common outcomes the OR overstates the RR.
cards.ex: Odds and risk diverge as the outcome becomes common.

cards.f: How can prevalence rise while incidence stays the same?
cards.b: Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration. A treatment that prolongs survival without cure lengthens duration, so more people are living with the disease at any time.
cards.ex: Antiretroviral therapy for HIV is the classic example.

cards.f: CER 20%, EER 15% over 5 years. NNT?
cards.b: ARR = 0.05, so NNT = 1/0.05 = 20 over 5 years.
cards.ex: NNT is 1/ARR, not 1/RRR or 1/CER.

cards.f: Same 25% RRR, but baseline 5-year risk 2%. NNT?
cards.b: Risk falls from 2% to 1.5%: ARR 0.005, NNT 200 over 5 years.
cards.ex: Lower baseline risk means a smaller ARR and a larger NNT.

cards.f: An SMR of 150 for a town
cards.b: There were 50% more deaths than expected if the town had the standard population's age-specific death rates.
cards.ex: SMR = observed ÷ expected × 100; 100 means as expected.

cards.f: Attributable fraction in the exposed vs population attributable fraction
cards.b: AF(exposed) = (RR − 1)/RR, the share of exposed cases due to the exposure. PAF also depends on how common the exposure is, giving the share of all cases in the population due to it.
cards.ex: A strong but rare exposure can have a high AF(exposed) and a small PAF.

cards.f: Incidence proportion vs incidence rate
cards.b: Incidence proportion (risk) divides new cases by people at risk at the start; incidence rate divides by person-time at risk, allowing for people followed for different lengths of time.
cards.ex: Rates suit cohorts with staggered entry or loss to follow-up.

cards.f: Number needed to treat
cards.b: 1 ÷ absolute risk reduction, rounded up, stated with the outcome and time period.
cards.ex: Always round up: you cannot treat part of a patient.

cards.f: A risk ratio of 0.8 with 95% CI 0.6 to 1.1
cards.b: A point estimate of 20% lower risk, but the interval includes 1, so the data are compatible with no effect (and with up to a 40% reduction or a 10% increase).
cards.ex: For ratios, the null value is 1, not 0.

cards.f: Sensitivity and specificity
cards.b: Sensitivity = TP/(TP + FN): proportion of diseased people who test positive. Specificity = TN/(TN + FP): proportion of non-diseased who test negative.
cards.ex: Sensitivity is about the diseased column; specificity the non-diseased column.

cards.f: Why does PPV fall when prevalence falls?
cards.b: With fewer diseased people there are fewer true positives, while the large healthy group still produces false positives at the same rate, so false positives make up more of the positive results.
cards.ex: Specificity applies to the healthy majority; in rare disease that majority dominates.

cards.f: Prevalence 1%, sensitivity 90%, specificity 95%, 10,000 screened. PPV?
cards.ex: Build the table with natural frequencies first: 100 diseased, 9,900 not.

cards.f: Lead-time bias vs length-time bias
cards.b: Lead-time: diagnosis moved earlier, so survival from diagnosis looks longer without any delay in death. Length-time: screening preferentially finds slow-growing, better-prognosis disease.
cards.ex: One concerns timing; the other, which cases get detected.

cards.f: Why is mortality in an RCT the right outcome for screening?
cards.b: Survival from diagnosis is inflated by lead-time, length-time and overdiagnosis; comparing deaths in randomised invited and uninvited groups avoids these biases.
cards.ex: Randomisation also removes healthy-volunteer bias.

cards.f: Screening vs case-finding
cards.b: Screening systematically invites a defined population without symptoms; case-finding opportunistically tests people already in contact with health services for another reason.
cards.ex: Both target people without symptoms of the condition; the difference is the systematic invitation.

cards.f: Likelihood ratio for a positive test
cards.b: LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); for 90% and 95% it is 0.9/0.05 = 18.
cards.ex: LRs do not depend on prevalence, unlike predictive values.

cards.f: What is overdiagnosis?
cards.b: Detecting disease that would never have caused symptoms or death in the person's lifetime; those people get labelled and treated, with harms but no benefit.
cards.ex: It is not a false positive: the disease is really there.

cards.f: A programme reports 5-year survival rising from 50% to 70% after screening began. Does this prove it saves lives?
cards.b: No: lead-time and length-time bias and overdiagnosis can raise survival with no change in deaths. You need mortality data, ideally from an RCT.
cards.ex: Survival statistics are not mortality statistics.

cards.f: May 2026: what did the UK NSC recommend about prostate cancer screening?
cards.b: Not to screen all men or Black men as a group; targeted two-yearly PSA testing for men aged 45 to 61 with a BRCA2 variant and relevant family history (England rollout expected from 2027).
cards.ex: Guidance changes: check the UK NSC for the current position.

cards.f: Standard deviation vs standard error
cards.b: SD describes the spread of individual observations; SE = SD/√n describes how precisely a sample mean estimates the population mean, and falls as n rises.
cards.ex: SD is about the data; SE is about the estimate.
Divide SD by √n first, then multiply by 1.96.

cards.f: Definition of a p-value
cards.b: The probability of obtaining a result at least as extreme as observed if the null hypothesis were true.
cards.ex: It is conditional on the null being true, so it cannot be the probability that the null is true.

cards.f: Type I vs type II error
cards.b: Type I: concluding there is an effect when there is none (false positive, probability α). Type II: missing a real effect (false negative, probability β).
cards.ex: Power = 1 − β.

cards.f: Why does a non-significant result not prove there is no effect?
cards.b: The study may be underpowered: the CI can still include clinically important effects. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
cards.ex: Always read the width of the confidence interval.

cards.f: How does sample size affect a confidence interval?
cards.b: The width is proportional to SE = SD/√n, so quadrupling n halves the width.
cards.ex: Precision improves with the square root of n, not n itself.

cards.f: Comparing 30-day readmission (yes/no) between two independent groups of 400. Which test?
cards.b: Chi-squared test (Fisher's exact test if expected counts are small).
cards.ex: Binary outcome in independent groups means a test of proportions.

cards.f: Comparing pain scores (skewed) before and after treatment in the same patients. Which test?
cards.b: Wilcoxon signed-rank test: paired data that are not normally distributed.
cards.ex: Paired plus skewed points to Wilcoxon signed-rank.

cards.f: Why do multiple comparisons inflate false positives?
cards.b: Each test has a chance α of a false positive, so with many tests the chance of at least one rises (20 tests at 0.05 give about one by chance). Bonferroni divides α by the number of tests.
cards.ex: Pre-specify a primary outcome to avoid this.

cards.f: Hazard ratio 0.79, 95% CI 0.64 to 0.97
cards.b: At any time, the event rate in the treated group is about 21% lower; the CI excludes 1, so this is statistically significant at the 5% level, but the true effect could be as small as a 3% reduction.
cards.ex: Hazard ratios compare event rates over time from Cox regression.

cards.f: Health inequality vs health inequity
cards.b: Inequality is any measurable difference in health between groups; inequity is a difference that is systematic, avoidable and unfair.
cards.ex: Age differences in health are inequalities but not necessarily inequities.

cards.f: What is the social gradient in health?
cards.b: Health worsens step by step down the socioeconomic scale across the whole population, not just among the poorest (shown in the Whitehall civil servant studies).
cards.ex: Even well-paid grades had worse health than the grade above.

cards.f: The Black Report's (1980) four explanations
cards.b: Artefact; natural or social selection; cultural or behavioural; materialist or structural (favoured by the Report).
cards.ex: Mnemonic: A S C M.

cards.f: Why is the cultural/behavioural explanation incomplete?
cards.b: Behaviours such as smoking and diet are shaped by income, stress, environment and marketing, and the gradient persists after adjusting for them.
cards.ex: Ask what causes the behaviour: 'the causes of the causes'.

cards.f: The inverse care law
cards.b: Julian Tudor Hart (1971): the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need for it in the population served.
cards.ex: It operates most where care is exposed to market forces.

cards.f: What is proportionate universalism?
cards.b: Universal action, delivered with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage (Marmot Review, 2010).
cards.ex: Targeting only the bottom misses the gradient; universal-only action may widen gaps.

cards.f: A smoking-cessation app raises quit rates overall but mostly among graduates. What has happened?
cards.b: Intervention-generated inequality: average health improved but the gap widened because uptake depended on individual resources.
cards.ex: Measure effects by group, not just on average.

cards.f: Core20PLUS5: what is the Core20?
cards.b: The most deprived 20% of the national population, as identified by the Index of Multiple Deprivation.
cards.ex: PLUS groups are chosen locally; the 5 are clinical areas.

cards.f: Name the five clinical areas in adult Core20PLUS5
cards.b: Maternity; severe mental illness (physical health checks); chronic respiratory disease; early cancer diagnosis; hypertension case-finding and lipid management.
cards.ex: Guidance may change; check NHS England.

cards.f: Dahlgren and Whitehead's rainbow: where does housing sit?
cards.b: In the living and working conditions layer, outside the individual-lifestyle and social-network layers and inside the general socioeconomic, cultural and environmental conditions.
cards.ex: Inner layers are fixed individual factors; outer layers are the wider determinants.

cards.f: The four principles (Beauchamp and Childress)
cards.b: Respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice; each is prima facie, so they must be weighed when they conflict.
cards.ex: Gillon added attention to scope.

cards.f: Act vs rule utilitarianism
cards.b: Act utilitarianism judges each act by its consequences; rule utilitarianism follows rules whose general observance maximises good, even when breaking one would help in a single case.
cards.ex: Confidentiality is easier to defend with rule utilitarianism.

cards.f: What does 'prima facie' mean for the four principles?
cards.b: Each principle binds unless it conflicts with another; then the clinician must judge which weighs more in the circumstances, rather than applying a fixed ranking.
cards.ex: There is no automatic priority of autonomy.

cards.f: Conditions of the doctrine of double effect
cards.b: Act good or neutral; only the good effect intended; bad effect not the means to the good; proportionate reason for allowing the bad effect.
cards.ex: All four must be met.

cards.f: Withdrawing artificial nutrition from a patient in a prolonged disorder of consciousness: act or omission in English law?
cards.b: Lawful when continuing is no longer in the patient's best interests: it allows the existing condition to take its course (Airedale NHS Trust v Bland, 1993). Positive action to end life is unlawful.
cards.ex: Bland is the leading acts/omissions case.

cards.f: Why is deontology a strong basis for consent?
cards.b: Kant's principle that people must never be treated merely as a means requires respecting their rational choices, so treatment without consent is wrong even if it produces good outcomes.
cards.ex: Consequences do not license using a person without consent.

cards.f: QALY maximisation vs the rule of rescue
cards.b: QALY maximisation spends to gain the most health per pound across the population; the rule of rescue is the urge to save identifiable people in peril regardless of cost.
cards.ex: The tension appears in funding requests for rare-disease drugs.

cards.f: Accountability for reasonableness (Daniels and Sabin): a procedural or a substantive test?
cards.b: Procedural: it does not say which treatments to fund, but requires that rationing decisions be public, based on relevant reasons, open to appeal and revision, and enforced.
cards.ex: It judges the fairness of the process when people disagree about outcomes.

cards.f: Is assisted dying lawful in England and Wales (October 2026)?
cards.b: No. Assisting suicide is an offence (s2 Suicide Act 1961); the 2024-25 bill fell in the Lords and the 2026-27 bill was defeated at Commons second reading in September 2026.
cards.ex: Check for any new bill.

cards.f: A capacitous patient refuses a life-saving blood transfusion. What do ethics and law say?
cards.b: Respect the refusal: a capacitous adult may refuse any treatment (Re T 1992; Ms B 2002). Check capacity, information and voluntariness, explore reasons and alternatives, and document.
cards.ex: Disagreement with the doctor is not evidence of incapacity.

cards.f: The four abilities in the MCA functional test (s3)
cards.b: Understand the relevant information; retain it; use or weigh it in deciding; communicate the decision by any means.
cards.ex: Failing any one means the person is unable to decide, if caused by an impairment of mind or brain.

cards.f: Order of questions when assessing capacity after JB (2021)?
cards.b: Functional question first (can they understand, retain, use or weigh, communicate?), then whether any inability is caused by an impairment of the mind or brain.
cards.ex: Starting with the diagnosis invites the assumption that dementia means incapacity.

cards.f: Montgomery test of a material risk
cards.b: A risk a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to, or one the doctor knows (or should know) this patient would.
cards.ex: It is patient-centred, not set by what other doctors would disclose.

cards.f: Montgomery vs McCulloch
cards.b: Montgomery: disclose material risks and reasonable alternatives. McCulloch: which alternatives are 'reasonable' is set by the professional practice test (Bolam).
cards.ex: Disclosure is patient-centred; identifying reasonable options is professional judgement.

cards.f: Why can't a 'next of kin' consent for an adult who lacks capacity?
cards.b: The term has no legal standing under the MCA; only an LPA attorney or court deputy (within their authority) can decide, otherwise the clinician decides in best interests after consulting family.
cards.ex: Family are consulted, not in charge.

cards.f: A patient wants an advance decision refusing ventilation even if her life is at risk. What makes it valid?
cards.b: In writing, signed, witnessed, with an express statement that it applies even if life is at risk; maker 18 or over with capacity when made.
cards.ex: Without the statement it does not cover life-sustaining treatment.

cards.f: Gillick competence vs Fraser guidelines
cards.b: Gillick: an under-16 can consent if they have enough maturity and understanding. Fraser: specific criteria for giving contraceptive advice or treatment without parental involvement.
cards.ex: Fraser is a subset applying to contraception.

cards.f: A patient with uncontrolled epilepsy keeps driving despite advice. Steps?
cards.b: Persuade; explain you may have to disclose; if they continue, tell them you will inform the DVLA, inform the DVLA medical adviser, then confirm in writing and record it.
cards.ex: The legal duty to notify the DVLA is the driver's; the GMC allows disclosure for public safety.

cards.f: How did the Supreme Court change the deprivation of liberty test in June 2026?
cards.b: It overruled the Cheshire West acid test; there is now a multifactorial assessment of the person's concrete situation, and someone lacking capacity may give or withhold valid consent by wishes and feelings.
cards.ex: Guidance and practice are still adjusting; check current guidance.

cards.f: A patient with capacity chooses a risky option against advice. Does this suggest incapacity?
cards.b: No. An unwise decision does not of itself show incapacity (s1(4)); assess the functional abilities for that decision.
cards.ex: Capacity is about the process of deciding, not the outcome.

cards.f: When may you disclose confidential information without consent in the public interest?
cards.b: Mainly to protect people from a risk of death or serious harm, when the benefit outweighs the harm to the patient and to trust; tell the patient first if safe, disclose the minimum and record it.
cards.ex: W v Egdell is the classic example.

cards.f: The four domains of Good medical practice 2024
cards.b: Knowledge, skills and development; patients, partnership and communication; colleagues, culture and safety; trust and professionalism.
cards.ex: In effect for doctors from 30 January 2024.

cards.f: Statutory vs professional duty of candour
cards.b: Statutory: Regulation 20, applies to registered organisations after notifiable safety incidents. Professional: GMC/NMC guidance, applies to every individual whenever something goes wrong.
cards.ex: Organisation vs individual; threshold vs any error.

cards.f: Why doesn't apologising mean admitting negligence?
cards.b: Section 2 Compensation Act 2006 says an apology or offer of redress does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence or breach of statutory duty.
cards.ex: Fear of liability is not a reason to withhold an apology.

cards.f: The five tasks of the Calgary-Cambridge guide
cards.b: Initiating the session; gathering information; building the relationship; giving information (explaining and planning); closing the session.
cards.ex: In the expanded guide, building the relationship and providing structure run through the whole consultation.

cards.f: You must break bad news. What do you do first, before giving the news?
cards.b: Prepare (notes, private room, companion offered, no interruptions), then find out what the patient knows and how much they want to know, then give a warning shot.
cards.ex: Perception and invitation come before knowledge.

cards.f: An FY1 smells alcohol on a registrar about to operate. Actions?
cards.b: Patient safety first: stop the registrar operating if possible, escalate immediately to the consultant or most senior available, record facts, follow local policy, and support the colleague's health.
cards.ex: Seniority is no reason to stay silent.

cards.f: Gross negligence manslaughter (Adomako) vs civil negligence
cards.b: Both need a duty and a breach; manslaughter also needs the breach to have caused death and to be so gross, in all the circumstances, that it deserves criminal punishment.
cards.ex: Grossness is a question for the jury.

cards.f: What did the Court of Appeal decide in Bawa-Garba v GMC (2018)?
cards.b: It set aside erasure and restored the tribunal's suspension: appeal courts should be slow to overturn a specialist tribunal's evaluative judgment, which could weigh systemic failings.
cards.ex: Not a ruling on the conviction itself.

cards.f: Why use a professional interpreter rather than a family member?
cards.b: Accuracy (medical terms, no filtering), confidentiality, and protecting the relative from an inappropriate role; children should never interpret.
cards.ex: Family may soften or withhold bad news.

cards.f: What does 'chunk and check' achieve?
cards.b: Giving information in small pieces and checking understanding before moving on prevents overload and reveals misunderstandings early.
cards.ex: Teach-back is the strongest way to check.

questions.q: Which study design selects participants on the basis of whether they already have the outcome of interest?
questions.why: A case-control study samples cases (with the outcome) and controls (without), then compares past exposures. That is why it is efficient for rare outcomes and gives an odds ratio.
optWhy: Correct: sampling by outcome defines the case-control design.
A cohort selects by exposure and follows people to see who develops the outcome.
A cross-sectional survey samples a population at one time point, measuring exposure and outcome together, without choosing people because of their outcome.
An RCT recruits eligible people and allocates the intervention at random; it does not select on outcome.
questions.clue: Selected on the basis of whether they already have the outcome.
questions.concept: Case-control studies sample by outcome; cohorts sample by exposure.

followUp.q: Researchers take 2,000 nurses who work nights and 2,000 who do not, and record new cases of breast cancer over 15 years. What is this design?
followUp.why: People are chosen by exposure (night work) and followed forward to count new outcomes, which is a prospective cohort. A case-control study would start from women with and without breast cancer; an ecological study compares groups such as regions; a cross-sectional study measures everything at one time.

questions.q: Researchers want to investigate possible causes of a very rare cancer with a long latent period of 20 to 30 years. Funding is limited. Which design is most efficient?
questions.why: Case-control studies sample on outcome, so enough cases of a rare disease can be assembled from registries without following huge populations for decades. Past exposures are then compared with suitable controls.
optWhy: A prospective cohort would need to follow very large numbers for decades to accumulate enough cases, which is slow and expensive.
Correct: efficient for rare outcomes and long latency because it starts from the cases.
Random allocation of a suspected cause would be unethical, and the trial would need to run for decades.
Ecological data can generate hypotheses but cannot show that exposed individuals develop the cancer (ecological fallacy).
A one-off survey would find very few prevalent cases of a rare cancer and could not establish whether exposure came first.
questions.clue: A very rare cancer, a long latent period and limited funding.
questions.concept: Case-control designs suit rare outcomes and long latency.

followUp.q: A cardiologist wants to measure how often heart failure develops, over 10 years, in people with and without type 2 diabetes, and to look at several outcomes. Which design fits best?
followUp.why: Measuring incidence in exposed and unexposed groups, and studying several outcomes of one exposure, are the strengths of a cohort study. A case-control study cannot give incidence, a case series has no comparison group, and an ecological study works at group level.

questions.q: An observational study finds that people who drink more alcohol have a higher rate of lung cancer. Heavy drinkers in the study were also much more likely to smoke. Which best explains the association?
options: Selection bias from loss to follow-up
questions.why: Smoking is associated with drinking, independently causes lung cancer, and does not lie on a causal path from alcohol to lung cancer, so it meets all three criteria for a confounder. Stratifying by smoking or adjusting for it would be expected to shrink the alcohol effect.
optWhy: Recall bias is an error in how exposures are reported; nothing in the stem suggests cases and non-cases remembered drinking differently.
Nothing in the stem describes losing participants, and loss to follow-up would not explain why drinkers also smoke.
Reverse causation would need lung cancer to cause heavier drinking, which is not plausible here.
Correct: smoking meets all three criteria for a confounder.
Lead-time bias concerns screening making survival look longer; it has nothing to do with this association.
questions.clue: Heavy drinkers were also much more likely to smoke.
questions.concept: A confounder is linked to the exposure, independently causes the outcome and is not on the causal pathway.

followUp.q: A study finds coffee drinkers have more myocardial infarctions, but within smokers and within non-smokers separately there is no difference. What has stratification shown?
options: Coffee causes infarction only in smokers
The coffee association was confounded by smoking
followUp.why: When the association disappears within each stratum of a third variable, that variable (smoking) was confounding the crude result. An effect only in smokers would be effect modification; recall bias and power are not shown by stratification.

questions.q: In a trial, 20% of patients randomised to a new drug stop taking it because of side effects. The authors report only patients who completed treatment, showing a large benefit. What is the main concern?
options: The trial should have been a case-control study
The analysis is per-protocol, which can exaggerate benefit by breaking randomisation
Blinding is impossible in drug trials
The result is affected by the ecological fallacy
questions.why: Excluding people who stopped treatment removes a non-random group (often those with side effects or more severe disease), so the remaining arms are no longer comparable. Intention-to-treat analysis keeps everyone in their randomised group and preserves the benefit of randomisation.
optWhy: A case-control design is weaker for testing a treatment; the RCT design is right, but the analysis is flawed.
Correct: dropping non-completers leaves arms that are no longer comparable.
Drug trials can usually be blinded with matching placebos.
The ecological fallacy concerns group-level data, not individual trial participants.
Intention-to-treat tends to give a conservative estimate of efficacy; 'always underestimates harm' is not a recognised rule and is not the issue here.
questions.clue: Only patients who completed treatment were analysed after 20% stopped.
questions.concept: Intention-to-treat analysis preserves randomisation.

followUp.q: In a surgical trial, 15 patients randomised to surgery decline the operation and receive medical treatment. In an intention-to-treat analysis, which group are they analysed in?
followUp.why: Intention-to-treat analyses everyone in the arm they were randomised to, whatever they actually received, so these patients stay in the surgery group. Moving them or excluding them would be an as-treated or per-protocol analysis and would break randomisation.

questions.q: Distinguish bias from confounding, giving a clinical example of each, and state one way of dealing with each. (5 marks)
markScheme: Bias is systematic error in the selection of participants or the measurement of exposure or outcome
Valid example of bias (e.g. recall bias in mothers of babies with birth defects)
Confounding is distortion by a third factor associated with the exposure, independently associated with the outcome and not on the causal pathway
Valid example of confounding (e.g. smoking confounding the alcohol and lung cancer association)
Bias is mainly prevented by design (e.g. objective records, blinding); confounding can be prevented by randomisation, restriction or matching, or adjusted for in analysis if measured
questions.modelAnswer: Bias is systematic error arising from how participants are selected or how information is collected. For example, in a case-control study of birth defects, mothers of affected babies may recall medicine use in pregnancy more thoroughly than control mothers (recall bias). It is mainly prevented by design, for example using prescription records instead of memory, or blinding outcome assessors. Confounding is a mixing of effects: a third variable is associated with the exposure, independently associated with the outcome, and is not on the causal pathway. Heavy drinkers smoke more, so an apparent link between alcohol and lung cancer may be due to smoking. Confounding can be prevented by randomisation, restriction or matching, or adjusted for in the analysis by stratification or multivariable models, provided the confounder was measured.
questions.concept: Bias is error in method; confounding is a real third variable; each has different remedies.

questions.q: In a case-control study, which measure of association can validly be calculated?
