questions.why: Because cases and controls are sampled in numbers the investigator chooses, the risk of disease in each exposure group cannot be estimated. The odds of exposure in cases versus controls can, and this odds ratio equals the odds ratio for disease.
optWhy: Correct: the odds ratio is valid whichever way the table is sampled.
Needs person-time at risk, which a case-control study does not measure.
Needs the risk in each exposure group, which case-control sampling does not provide.
NNT needs an absolute risk difference, which also needs risks.
questions.clue: Case-control design.
questions.concept: Odds ratios are the measure for case-control studies.

followUp.q: A cohort of 5,000 workers is followed for 10 years and the risk of asthma is compared in exposed and unexposed workers. Which ratio is the natural summary?
followUp.why: A cohort measures risk in each exposure group, so the risk ratio is the natural measure (an odds ratio could also be calculated but is not needed). An SMR compares observed with expected deaths, and a likelihood ratio describes a diagnostic test.

questions.q: In a trial, 20% of patients in the placebo group and 15% in the treatment group have a stroke over five years. What is the number needed to treat to prevent one stroke over five years?
questions.why: ARR = 20% − 15% = 5 percentage points = 0.05. NNT = 1/0.05 = 20, so 20 people must be treated for five years to prevent one stroke.
optWhy: 1/0.20 uses the control event rate instead of the absolute risk reduction.
1/0.25 uses the relative risk reduction (5/20 = 25%) instead of the absolute reduction.
25 is the relative risk reduction expressed as a number (25%), not an NNT.
1/0.15 = 6.7, rounded up to 7, uses the treatment-group event rate.
questions.clue: Event rates of 20% and 15% over five years.
questions.concept: NNT = 1/ARR.

followUp.q: The same drug (same 25% relative risk reduction) is used in people whose 5-year stroke risk is 2%. What is the NNT over five years?
followUp.why: Risk falls from 2% to 1.5%, so ARR = 0.005 and NNT = 200. 20 assumes the original baseline risk; 50 is 1/0.02 (the baseline risk); 4 is 1/RRR.

questions.q: A case-control study of hip fracture in adults over 70 recruits 100 cases and 200 controls. Sixty cases and 50 controls report regular use of a sleeping tablet. What is the odds ratio for fracture associated with use?
questions.why: Odds of exposure in cases = 60/40 = 1.5; in controls = 50/150 ≈ 0.33. OR = 1.5 ÷ 0.33 = 4.5 (equivalently ad/bc = 60 × 150 ÷ (40 × 50) = 9,000/2,000).
optWhy: Divides exposed cases by exposed controls (60/50), ignoring the unexposed.
This is the odds of exposure among cases only (60/40), not a ratio of odds.
Divides the proportions exposed (0.60/0.25), which treats exposure prevalence like a risk; risks cannot be estimated in a case-control study.
This is the reciprocal (1/4.5), from inverting the table.
questions.clue: Numbers of exposed and unexposed cases and controls are given.
questions.concept: OR = ad/bc in a case-control study.

followUp.q: In another case-control study, 30 of 50 cases and 20 of 100 controls were exposed. What is the odds ratio?
followUp.why: Odds in cases = 30/20 = 1.5; in controls = 20/80 = 0.25; OR = 6.0. 3.0 is the ratio of proportions exposed (0.6/0.2); 1.5 is the odds in cases alone; 0.17 is the inverted ratio.

questions.q: An advertisement says a new tablet 'halves the risk of hip fracture'. In the trial, fractures over 3 years fell from 2 per 1,000 to 1 per 1,000. Which statement best describes the benefit for a patient?
options: About 1,000 people need to take it for 3 years to prevent one fracture
Half of the people who take it will avoid a fracture
The number needed to treat is 2
questions.why: ARR = 2/1,000 − 1/1,000 = 1/1,000 = 0.001, so NNT = 1,000 over 3 years. The 50% is the relative risk reduction, which sounds large because the baseline risk is low.
optWhy: Correct: NNT = 1/0.001 = 1,000 over 3 years.
50% is the relative risk reduction; the absolute reduction is 0.1 percentage points.
Confuses the relative risk reduction with the proportion of people who benefit; most would never have had a fracture anyway.
1/0.5 uses the relative risk reduction instead of the absolute risk reduction.
The risk ratio (treated ÷ control) is 0.5, not 2.0; 2.0 inverts it.
questions.clue: 'Halves the risk' when the baseline is 2 per 1,000.
questions.concept: Relative effects need absolute risks and NNT to be meaningful.

followUp.q: In a high-risk group, an outcome occurs in 40% on control and 20% on treatment. What are the RRR and the NNT?
followUp.why: ARR = 0.40 − 0.20 = 0.20, so NNT = 5; RRR = 0.20/0.40 = 50%. Treating 20% as the RRR confuses absolute and relative reductions, and an NNT of 2 comes from 1/RRR.

questions.q: In a cohort study, 30 of 1,000 smokers and 20 of 2,000 non-smokers develop disease X. Calculate (a) the relative risk, (b) the risk difference, (c) the number needed to harm, (d) the attributable fraction among smokers, and (e) the population attributable fraction, and interpret (e). (5 marks)
markScheme: Risk difference = 2 percentage points (0.02)
NNH = 1/0.02 = 50 over the study period
AF in the exposed = (3 − 1)/3 ≈ 67%
PAF = 0.4 (40%), e.g. (1/3 × 2)/(1 + 2/3), checked by (1.67% − 1%)/1.67%; if causal, 40% of all cases are due to smoking
questions.modelAnswer: Risk in smokers = 30/1,000 = 3%; risk in non-smokers = 20/2,000 = 1%. (a) RR = 3/1 = 3. (b) Risk difference = 3% − 1% = 2 percentage points. (c) NNH = 1/0.02 = 50: for every 50 people who smoke, one extra case occurs over the study period. (d) Attributable fraction among smokers = (RR − 1)/RR = 2/3 ≈ 67%. (e) The proportion exposed is 1,000/3,000 = 1/3, so PAF = (1/3 × 2)/(1 + 2/3) = 0.4. Check: overall risk = 50/3,000 ≈ 1.67%, and (1.67 − 1)/1.67 ≈ 0.4. If the association is causal, 40% of cases in this population are attributable to smoking and would be avoided if nobody smoked.
questions.concept: Calculating risk-based measures and attributable fractions from cohort data.

questions.q: Which measure of a screening test's performance changes when the same test is used in a population with a different prevalence?
questions.why: PPV = TP/(TP + FP). As prevalence falls there are fewer true positives relative to false positives, so PPV falls, even though the test's sensitivity and specificity are unchanged.
optWhy: Sensitivity is calculated only among people who have the disease, so it does not depend on how many people have it.
Correct: predictive values depend on prevalence.
Specificity is calculated only among people without the disease, so it does not depend on prevalence either.
The likelihood ratio is built from sensitivity and specificity, so it does not change with prevalence.
questions.clue: The same test is used in a population with a different prevalence.
questions.concept: Predictive values depend on prevalence; sensitivity and specificity do not.

followUp.q: A test with fixed sensitivity and specificity is moved from a specialist clinic (prevalence 30%) to population screening (prevalence 0.5%). What happens to its NPV?
followUp.why: With very few diseased people, almost every negative result is a true negative, so NPV rises (and PPV falls). It is not unchanged, because predictive values depend on prevalence, and it does not simply equal specificity.

questions.q: A new blood test for a cancer has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. It is used to screen 10,000 asymptomatic adults in whom prevalence is 1%. Approximately what proportion of people with a positive result actually have the cancer?
questions.why: 100 people have the cancer, giving 90 true positives. Of 9,900 without it, 5% (495) test positive. PPV = 90/(90 + 495) = 90/585 ≈ 15%.
optWhy: This is the sensitivity, which is the proportion of people with cancer who test positive, not the proportion of positives who have cancer.
Correct: 90 true positives out of 585 positives.
This is the specificity, the proportion of people without cancer who test negative.
A guess that ignores prevalence; there are over five false positives for each true positive.
This is the prevalence, the pre-test probability, not the post-test probability.
questions.clue: Sensitivity 90%, specificity 95%, prevalence 1% in asymptomatic adults.
questions.concept: PPV is low when prevalence is low.

followUp.q: The same test (sensitivity 90%, specificity 95%) is used in a symptomatic clinic of 1,000 people where prevalence is 10%. What is the PPV?
followUp.why: 100 have the cancer: TP 90. 900 do not: FP 45. PPV = 90/135 ≈ 67%. About 15% is the PPV at 1% prevalence; 90% is the sensitivity; about 99% is close to the NPV.

questions.q: Five-year survival after diagnosis of a cancer rose from 40% to 65% after a screening programme was introduced, but the death rate from that cancer in the population did not change. Which explanation best fits?
questions.why: If deaths are unchanged but survival from diagnosis rises, diagnosis has simply been moved earlier (lead time) and more indolent or never-harmful cases are being counted (length-time bias and overdiagnosis), inflating survival without saving lives.
optWhy: Better treatment would be expected to reduce the death rate, which did not change.
Age confounding could affect comparisons between populations, but it would not explain rising survival with a stable death rate in the same population.
Recall bias concerns participants' memory of exposures in case-control studies.
Correct: earlier and extra diagnoses inflate survival with no fall in deaths.
Specificity affects false positives; it does not explain the gap between survival and mortality.
questions.clue: Survival rose but the death rate did not change.
questions.concept: Survival from diagnosis is biased by lead time, length time and overdiagnosis.

followUp.q: Screening for a slow-growing tumour finds many cases that would never have caused symptoms. What is this called?
followUp.why: Finding real disease that would never have harmed the person is overdiagnosis. It is not a false positive, because the disease is present; lead-time bias concerns earlier timing; healthy volunteer bias concerns who attends.

questions.q: A private company proposes annual whole-body scans for healthy adults to 'find disease early'. Which is the strongest reason the UK NSC would not recommend such a programme?
options: There is no randomised evidence that it reduces mortality or morbidity, and harms such as overdiagnosis and false positives are likely
Scans are less sensitive than blood tests
Adults cannot give informed consent to screening
Screening is only allowed for cancers
questions.why: The UK NSC's central requirement is high-quality evidence, ideally from RCTs, that a programme reduces mortality or morbidity and that benefits outweigh harms. Untargeted scanning finds many incidental, often harmless findings that lead to further tests and anxiety.
optWhy: Cost matters (value for money is one criterion), but cost alone is not the main objection.
Correct: the evidence of benefit is missing and harms are likely.
Relative sensitivity is not the issue, and scans are often very sensitive, which increases incidental findings.
Capacitous adults can consent to screening; informed choice is in fact a UK NSC requirement.
UK programmes include non-cancer conditions such as abdominal aortic aneurysm, diabetic eye disease and newborn conditions.
questions.clue: Healthy adults, untargeted scans, 'find disease early'.
questions.concept: UK NSC criteria require evidence that benefit outweighs harm.

followUp.q: Which of these is one of the UK NSC criteria for a screening programme?
options: People must receive information that supports an informed choice
The condition must be a cancer
followUp.why: Providing understandable information so that people can make an informed choice is a UK NSC criterion. No test is required to be perfect, there is no fixed uptake target in the criteria, and screened conditions are not limited to cancers.

questions.q: Explain lead-time bias, length-time bias and overdiagnosis in screening, and state what kind of evidence avoids them. (4 marks)
markScheme: Lead-time bias: earlier diagnosis lengthens apparent survival from diagnosis without delaying death
Length-time bias: slow-growing disease spends longer in the detectable phase, so screening over-detects favourable-prognosis cases
Overdiagnosis: detecting disease that would never have caused symptoms or death, leading to unnecessary treatment
RCT comparing disease-specific (or overall) mortality between invited and uninvited groups avoids these biases
questions.modelAnswer: Lead-time bias: screening moves the date of diagnosis earlier, so survival measured from diagnosis looks longer even if the person dies when they would have died without screening. Length-time bias: indolent tumours stay in the pre-clinical detectable phase longer than aggressive ones, so screen-detected cases are weighted towards better prognosis. Overdiagnosis: screening finds disease, such as some ductal carcinoma in situ or low-grade prostate cancer, that would never have caused symptoms or death. Those people receive treatment and its harms without benefit. All three make screening look more effective than it is. The proper evidence is a randomised trial comparing mortality (not survival from diagnosis) in people invited and not invited to screening.
questions.concept: Biases in evaluating screening and why RCT mortality is the outcome.

questions.q: A trial reports p = 0.03 for its primary outcome. Which statement is correct?
options: There is a 97% chance the treatment works
There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
If there were truly no difference, results at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
The treatment effect is clinically important
questions.why: A p-value is calculated assuming the null hypothesis is true: it is the probability of data at least as extreme as those observed under that assumption. It does not give the probability that a hypothesis is true or how large the effect is.
optWhy: Treats 1 − p as the probability of benefit, which the p-value does not measure.
The p-value assumes the null is true; it cannot also be the probability that the null is true.
Correct: this is the definition of a p-value.
Statistical significance says nothing about the size or importance of the effect.
Power is decided before the study from sample size, effect size and α, not from the observed p-value.
questions.concept: The definition and limits of a p-value.

followUp.q: A trial reports a mean difference of 4 mmHg, 95% CI −1 to 9 mmHg. Which is the best interpretation?
options: The result is significant at the 5% level
The true effect is exactly 4 mmHg
The data are compatible with no effect and with a benefit of up to 9 mmHg
followUp.why: The interval includes 0 (the null value for a difference), so p > 0.05, but it also includes worthwhile benefits; the honest conclusion is uncertainty. It does not prove no effect, it is not significant, and 4 mmHg is only the point estimate.

questions.q: An investigator compares the proportion of patients readmitted within 30 days (yes or no) between two independent groups of 400 patients each. Which test is most appropriate?
questions.why: The outcome is binary (readmitted or not) and the groups are independent, so a chi-squared test comparing two proportions fits. Fisher's exact test is used instead if expected counts are small, which is unlikely with 400 per group.
optWhy: A paired t-test compares means of continuous data measured twice in the same people.
Correct: proportions in independent groups.
Wilcoxon signed-rank is for paired, non-normal continuous or ordinal data.
Pearson correlation measures linear association between two continuous variables.
ANOVA compares means of a continuous outcome across three or more groups.
questions.clue: Binary outcome (yes or no) in two independent groups.
questions.concept: Matching the test to the data type and design.

followUp.q: Length of stay (strongly right-skewed) is compared between two independent hospitals. Which test?
followUp.why: Skewed continuous data in two independent groups suit the Mann–Whitney U test. A t-test assumes approximately normal data; chi-squared is for categorical outcomes; a paired test needs matched observations.

questions.q: In a sample of 36 adults the mean systolic blood pressure is 140 mmHg with standard deviation 12 mmHg. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the population mean?
optWhy: Uses the SD instead of the SE (140 ± 1.96 × 12): this is the range containing about 95% of individuals, not the CI for the mean.
Uses an SE of 1, which would need n = 144.
Correct: mean ± 1.96 × SD/√n.
Uses ± 1 SD (140 ± 12), which describes individual variability.
Divides the SD by n (12/36) instead of √n.
questions.clue: SD 12 and n = 36 are both given.
questions.concept: CI for a mean = mean ± 1.96 × SD/√n.

followUp.q: With the same mean and SD but a sample of 144, what is the approximate 95% CI?
followUp.why: SE = 12/√144 = 1, so 140 ± 1.96 ≈ 138.0 to 142.0. Quadrupling the sample halves the width. 136.1 to 143.9 is the n = 36 answer; 139.0 to 141.0 uses ± 1 SE; 116.5 to 163.5 uses the SD.

questions.q: A trial reports 20 secondary outcomes. One shows p = 0.04; the other 19 are not significant. The press release highlights this outcome as a new benefit. What is the main problem?
options: With 20 tests, about one p < 0.05 is expected by chance (multiple testing)
The result is a type II error
The study should have used a case-control design
A p-value of 0.04 proves the result is clinically important
questions.why: At α = 0.05, roughly 1 in 20 tests will be 'significant' by chance when there is no real effect. A single significant secondary outcome among 20 should be treated as hypothesis-generating; a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold would be 0.05/20 = 0.0025.
optWhy: Correct: multiple testing inflates false positives.
A type II error is missing a real effect; the concern here is a false positive (type I).
Nothing in the stem gives a CI; a p of 0.04 would correspond to a 95% CI that excludes the null value.
The design is not the issue; selective reporting of many tests is.
Significance does not establish clinical importance, and here the result may be chance.
questions.clue: 20 secondary outcomes, one with p = 0.04.
questions.concept: Multiple testing and the Bonferroni correction.

followUp.q: Five subgroup analyses are planned. Using the Bonferroni method with overall α = 0.05, what p-value threshold applies to each?
followUp.why: Bonferroni divides α by the number of tests: 0.05/5 = 0.01. Keeping 0.05 ignores multiplicity; 0.25 multiplies instead of dividing; 0.005 would be for ten tests.

questions.q: In a sample of 36 adults the mean systolic blood pressure is 140 mmHg with a standard deviation of 12 mmHg. (a) Calculate the standard error. (b) Calculate the 95% confidence interval for the mean. (c) Interpret the interval. (d) State how the interval would change if the sample were 144 people with the same SD. (4 marks)
markScheme: SE = 12/√36 = 2 mmHg
Interpretation: range of plausible values for the population mean; about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean
n = 144: SE = 1, CI halves in width to about 138.0 to 142.0 mmHg
questions.modelAnswer: (a) SE = SD/√n = 12/6 = 2 mmHg. (b) 95% CI = 140 ± 1.96 × 2 = 140 ± 3.92, which is 136.1 to 143.9 mmHg. (c) The interval gives a range of plausible values for the true population mean. If the sampling were repeated many times, about 95% of intervals built this way would contain the true mean. It does not describe where 95% of individuals lie, which would use the SD. (d) With n = 144, SE = 12/12 = 1, so the CI is 140 ± 1.96, about 138.0 to 142.0 mmHg. Quadrupling the sample halves the width.
questions.concept: Standard error and confidence interval for a mean.

questions.q: The 'inverse care law', stating that the availability of good medical care tends to vary inversely with the need for it, was described by:
questions.why: Julian Tudor Hart, a GP in a Welsh mining village, described the inverse care law in the Lancet in 1971, noting that it operates most fully where medical care is exposed to market forces.
optWhy: Correct: Tudor Hart, Lancet 1971.
Marmot's 2010 review introduced proportionate universalism and six policy objectives.
The Black Report (1980) set out four explanations of health inequalities, not the inverse care law.
Dahlgren and Whitehead produced the 'rainbow' model of determinants of health.
questions.clue: Availability of care varying inversely with need.
questions.concept: Key named concepts in health inequalities.

followUp.q: Which concept says that action should be universal but scaled in intensity to the level of disadvantage?
followUp.why: Proportionate universalism comes from the Marmot Review (2010). The inverse care law describes a problem rather than a remedy; social selection is a Black Report explanation; the rule of rescue concerns identifiable lives in resource allocation.

questions.q: A study finds that civil servants in middle grades, none of whom are poor, have higher coronary mortality than those in the top grade, and lower than those in the bottom grade. Adjusting for smoking explains only part of the difference. What does this best illustrate?
questions.why: Mortality rising step by step down the hierarchy, even among people who are not poor, is the social gradient (as in the Whitehall studies). That conventional risk factors explain only part of it points to wider material and psychosocial determinants.
optWhy: The data are on individuals, not area-level averages, so the ecological fallacy does not apply.
The inverse care law concerns access to care relative to need, not mortality across grades.
Correct: a stepwise gradient across the whole hierarchy.
Artefact would mean the finding came from measurement error; consistent gradients across measures argue against this.
Lead-time bias is a screening concept.
questions.clue: Middle grades who are not poor still do worse than the top grade.
questions.concept: The social gradient spans the whole population.

followUp.q: Life expectancy rises steadily with each decile of decreasing area deprivation, not just between the most deprived decile and the rest. This pattern is best described as:
followUp.why: A stepwise relationship across every decile is a social gradient. A threshold effect would show a difference only below a cut-off; reverse causation and regression to the mean are not described by this pattern.

questions.q: A practice introduces an online booking app for NHS Health Checks. Uptake rises overall, but mostly among affluent, younger patients; uptake in older patients and those needing interpreters is unchanged. What is the best description and response?
options: Successful intervention; no further action needed
Inverse care law; close the app
Ecological fallacy; analyse at area level
Selection bias; randomise patients to the app
Intervention-generated inequality; add proportionate measures such as phone and in-person booking and interpreter-supported outreach
questions.why: Interventions relying on individual resources (digital access, language) can widen gaps even as averages improve. Keeping the universal offer while adding more intensive routes for the groups being missed is proportionate universalism.
optWhy: Ignores that the gap between groups has widened.
Withdrawing a useful universal offer would reduce access for everyone rather than levelling up.
The data describe individual patients' uptake, so the ecological fallacy is not the issue.
This is a service evaluation, not a biased research sample; randomising would not fix unequal access.
Correct: names the problem and applies a proportionate-universalist fix.
questions.clue: Uptake rose mostly among affluent, younger patients.
questions.concept: Individual-agency interventions can widen inequalities; respond proportionately.

followUp.q: Which response best reflects proportionate universalism in a vaccination programme?
options: Offer vaccination only in the most deprived areas
Offer it to all with identical effort everywhere
Offer vaccination to all, with extra outreach, reminders and pop-up clinics where uptake is lowest
Charge a fee so that resources follow demand
followUp.why: Universal offer plus effort scaled to need is proportionate universalism. Targeting only deprived areas misses the gradient, identical effort ignores unequal barriers, and fees would worsen the inverse care law.

questions.q: A health board's report argues that inequalities in lung cancer mortality are 'simply because poorer people choose to smoke', so the only response needed is health education. Which Black Report explanation does this rely on, and what is its main weakness?
options: Cultural/behavioural; it ignores that smoking is socially patterned by stress, income, environment and marketing
questions.why: Attributing the gap to choices is the cultural/behavioural explanation. Behaviours are shaped by material and psychosocial circumstances (the causes of the causes), and education alone tends to be taken up by advantaged groups.
optWhy: The argument is about choices, not material conditions.
Artefact argues the gradient is a measurement product; the report does not question the data.
Correct: names the explanation and its key weakness.
Selection argues that illness causes downward mobility, which is not the argument made.
The argument does not invoke income at all.
questions.clue: 'Poorer people choose to smoke', so only health education is needed.
questions.concept: Black Report explanations and their critique.

followUp.q: 'People with chronic illness lose their jobs and move into poorer areas, so the illness causes the deprivation.' Which explanation is this?
followUp.why: Health causing social position is the selection (health selection) explanation. Artefact concerns measurement, cultural/behavioural concerns lifestyle differences, and materialist concerns circumstances causing ill health.

questions.q: Explain the concept of proportionate universalism and give one example of how it could be applied in the NHS. (4 marks)
markScheme: Originates from the Marmot Review 'Fair Society, Healthy Lives' (2010)
Actions are universal (offered to all)
Scale and intensity proportionate to level of disadvantage, because the social gradient affects everyone
Valid example, e.g. universal health visiting with additional visits for families with greater need; targeted outreach within a universal screening programme
questions.modelAnswer: Proportionate universalism comes from the Marmot Review, 'Fair Society, Healthy Lives' (2010). Focusing only on the most disadvantaged would miss the social gradient, which affects everyone below the top. So actions should be universal, but delivered with a scale and intensity proportionate to the level of disadvantage. For example, health visiting is offered to all families, with more frequent visits and linked support for families with greater need. Another example is adding text reminders, outreach and community champions to bowel screening in areas with low uptake while keeping the universal invitation.
questions.concept: Proportionate universalism as a response to the social gradient.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a condition of the doctrine of double effect?
options: The bad effect must not be the means by which the good effect is achieved
There must be a proportionate reason for allowing the bad effect
The patient must have given written consent to the bad effect
The act itself must be good or morally neutral
Only the good effect must be intended
questions.why: Double effect has four conditions: the act is good or neutral, only the good effect is intended, the bad effect is not the means to the good, and there is proportionate reason. Written consent is not one of them (although consent matters for other reasons).
optWhy: This is one of the conditions: the good must not be achieved through the bad.
This is the proportionality condition.
Correct: written consent is not a condition of double effect.
This is the condition about the nature of the act.
This is the intention condition: the bad effect may be foreseen but not intended.
questions.clue: The question asks which is NOT a condition.
questions.concept: The four conditions of double effect.

followUp.q: A doctor gives medication to relieve severe breathlessness in a dying patient, foreseeing it may slightly shorten life. Which feature is essential for double effect to apply?
options: The intention is to relieve symptoms, not to cause death, and the dose is proportionate to the symptoms
A second doctor signs the chart
The patient has less than 24 hours to live
followUp.why: Double effect turns on intention (relieving suffering) and proportionality. Family agreement, a second signature or a time limit are not conditions of double effect, though good practice includes discussion and documentation.

questions.q: A 34-year-old woman with capacity refuses a blood transfusion after a postpartum haemorrhage because of her religious beliefs. Her husband urges the team to transfuse. What should the team do?
options: Transfuse, because beneficence outweighs autonomy when life is at risk
Transfuse, because she has a duty to her baby
Ask the husband to consent on her behalf
Apply to the court for permission to transfuse because the refusal is irrational
Respect her refusal, confirm her capacity and that the decision is voluntary and informed, offer acceptable alternatives and document
questions.why: A capacitous adult may refuse any treatment, even life-saving, for any reason or none (Re T; Ms B). The team should confirm capacity, check she is free from undue pressure, ensure she understands the consequences, offer alternatives she accepts, and record everything.
optWhy: Beneficence cannot override a capacitous adult's informed refusal.
Her capacitous refusal binds the team; a duty she may feel towards her baby does not give doctors a legal power to override it.
No one can consent on behalf of a capacitous adult, and a spouse has no legal authority to do so.
An unwise or irrational-seeming decision does not by itself show incapacity; the court route is for genuine doubt about capacity or validity.
Correct: respect a capacitous, informed, voluntary refusal.
questions.clue: Capacity, a clear refusal and her husband's pressure.
questions.concept: Capacitous adults may refuse life-saving treatment.

followUp.q: Doctors suspect that a patient's refusal of treatment was produced by intense pressure from a relative. What is the legal concern?
options: Undue influence making the refusal not voluntary, which can make it invalid
The relative's legal right to decide
followUp.why: In Re T the court held that a refusal shaped by undue influence may not be a true, voluntary decision. A relative has no right to decide for a capacitous adult, and the issue here is voluntariness rather than capacity or confidentiality.

questions.q: An integrated care board declines to fund an expensive cancer drug for a 10-year-old after a published, reasoned process that weighed evidence and opportunity cost. The family seeks judicial review. On the basis of R v Cambridge Health Authority, ex parte B (1995), what is the court most likely to examine?
options: Whether the drug would work for this child
Whether the cost per QALY is below £20,000
Whether the decision-making process was lawful and rational, not the clinical merits
Whether the family has a right to any treatment they request
questions.why: In ex parte B the Court of Appeal held that courts cannot decide how a limited budget is best allocated; it upheld the authority's decision as within its powers. Judicial review asks whether the decision was lawful and rational, which fits the procedural fairness Daniels and Sabin describe.
optWhy: Courts generally do not substitute their own clinical judgement for the body's.
Thresholds are set by NICE for its appraisals; the court does not apply a fixed figure, and the current standard range is higher than this.
Correct: judicial review looks at legality and rationality of the process.
There is no legal right to demand any treatment regardless of resources.
Negligence is a different legal action about breach of a duty of care.
questions.clue: A reasoned, published funding decision challenged in court.
questions.concept: Courts review the fairness of rationing processes rather than their outcomes.

followUp.q: Which condition belongs to Daniels and Sabin's 'accountability for reasonableness'?
options: Decisions must be made by courts
Decisions and their reasons must be publicly available
followUp.why: Publicity is one of the four conditions (with relevance, revision/appeals and enforcement). QALY maximisation and the rule of rescue are substantive positions, not procedural conditions, and courts are not the decision-makers.

questions.q: A student argues: 'If breaking a confidence would prevent minor harm this once, we should do it, because the outcome is better.' Which framework is this, and what is the main objection?
options: Rule utilitarianism; it is too rigid
Act utilitarianism; it ignores the value of a general rule of confidentiality that keeps patients' trust
questions.why: Judging a single act by its outcome is act utilitarianism. A rule utilitarian, and the GMC, would point out that routinely breaching confidence for minor benefits would undermine trust and discourage disclosure, which leads to worse outcomes overall; disclosure is justified only for serious harm.
optWhy: The argument is outcome-based, which is the opposite of deontology.
Casuistry reasons from analogous cases; the argument does not.
The argument does not appeal to character.
Rule utilitarianism would generally support keeping the confidence here.
Correct: act utilitarianism, criticised for ignoring the benefit of the rule.
questions.clue: 'This once ... because the outcome is better.'
questions.concept: Act versus rule utilitarianism applied to confidentiality.

followUp.q: Which statement best represents a deontological view of lying to a patient to protect them from distress?
options: It is right if it reduces overall distress
It depends on what a virtuous doctor would feel
It is wrong because it fails to respect the patient as a rational agent, whatever the outcome
It is right if a rule allowing it would maximise welfare
followUp.why: Deontology holds that deception violates a duty to respect persons regardless of outcome. Outcome-based judgements are consequentialist (act or rule), and the virtue-based answer appeals to character.

questions.q: Explain the difference between act and rule utilitarianism, and show how each might approach a doctor's decision about breaching confidentiality to prevent minor harm to a third party. (4 marks)
markScheme: Act utilitarianism judges each individual act by its consequences
An act utilitarian might breach if the immediate net benefit seems greater
Rule utilitarianism follows rules whose general observance maximises good
A rule utilitarian would likely keep the confidence because a general rule of confidentiality sustains trust and disclosure; exceptions only for serious harm, as in GMC guidance
questions.modelAnswer: Act utilitarianism assesses each action by its own consequences: the right act maximises overall welfare in that situation. Faced with a chance to prevent minor harm to a third party, an act utilitarian might breach confidentiality if the immediate benefit seemed to outweigh the harm to the patient. Rule utilitarianism asks which general rules, if followed, produce the best outcomes. A rule of medical confidentiality encourages patients to seek care and disclose sensitive information, which benefits public health overall. So a rule utilitarian would keep the confidence where the threatened harm is minor, and allow exceptions only for serious harm. This mirrors GMC guidance, which permits disclosure in the public interest mainly to protect others from a risk of death or serious harm.
questions.concept: Act versus rule utilitarianism.

questions.q: Under s3 Mental Capacity Act 2005, which of the following is NOT one of the abilities a person must have to make a decision?
options: Use or weigh that information as part of the decision-making process
Understand the information relevant to the decision
Justify the decision to the clinician as rational
Communicate the decision by any means
questions.why: Section 3 lists understanding, retaining, using or weighing, and communicating. There is no requirement that the decision be rational or justified to the clinician; an unwise decision does not by itself show incapacity.
optWhy: Using or weighing it is one of the s3 abilities.
Understanding the relevant information is one of the s3 abilities.
Retaining it, even briefly, is one of the s3 abilities.
Correct: rational justification is not part of the test.
Communicating by any means is one of the s3 abilities.
questions.clue: The question asks which is NOT a s3 ability.
questions.concept: The four functional abilities in s3 MCA.

followUp.q: A patient can explain the risks of refusing dialysis immediately afterwards but forgets them within an hour. Can she have capacity to decide?
options: Yes, if she can retain it long enough to make the decision
No, she must retain information indefinitely
followUp.why: Section 3(3) says retaining information for a short period only does not prevent a person being able to decide. Indefinite retention is not required, relatives have no say over a capacitous patient, and forgetfulness alone does not prove incapacity.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman is offered a laparoscopic procedure. There is a 1 in 2,000 risk of nerve injury affecting her hand. She is a professional violinist. The surgeon does not mention the risk because most surgeons would not. Which statement best reflects the law in England and Wales?
options: No breach, because a responsible body of surgeons would not disclose (Bolam)
The procedure is a battery because a risk was not disclosed
Likely breach, because the surgeon knew or should have known this patient would attach significance to the risk (Montgomery)
Disclosure is only needed if she asks directly
questions.why: Under Montgomery a risk is material if a reasonable person in her position would attach significance to it, or the doctor knows or should know that this patient would. For a violinist, a small risk to hand function is plainly significant.
optWhy: Bolam no longer governs disclosure of risks after Montgomery.
She agreed to the broad nature of the procedure, so battery fails (Chatterton v Gerson); the claim would be in negligence.
Correct: the patient-specific limb of the materiality test applies.
Montgomery rejected reducing materiality to percentages.
Doctors must engage in dialogue; disclosure does not depend on the patient asking.
questions.clue: A rare risk to the hand in a professional violinist.
questions.concept: Montgomery's materiality test includes this patient's particular concerns.

followUp.q: A doctor did not mention an alternative treatment that she, supported by a responsible body of medical opinion, had judged unsuitable. Under McCulloch (2023), is this a breach?
options: Yes, every alternative must be mentioned
No, because patients cannot sue about alternatives
Yes, because Montgomery abolished Bolam entirely
No, because which alternatives are reasonable is decided by the professional practice test
followUp.why: McCulloch held that the professional practice test identifies the reasonable alternatives; options reasonably excluded need not be disclosed. Montgomery did not abolish Bolam for this question, and patients can sue if reasonable alternatives are not disclosed.

questions.q: Fifteen-year-old Jade asks her GP for contraception and does not want her parents told. She understands the advice, is in a relationship with a 16-year-old, will continue having sex regardless and cannot be persuaded to involve her parents. What should the GP do?
options: Refuse until a parent consents, because she is under 16
Inform her parents, because confidentiality does not apply to under-16s
Provide contraception only if she is 16 within a month
Assess Gillick competence and apply the Fraser guidelines; if met, provide contraception confidentially while checking for safeguarding concerns
Refer to the Court of Protection
questions.why: Under-16s can consent if Gillick competent, and the Fraser guidelines set the criteria for contraceptive advice without parental involvement. A competent young person is owed confidentiality, but the GP should still consider safeguarding (partner's age, coercion, exploitation) and document the assessment.
optWhy: There is no rule that under-16s always need parental consent (Gillick).
Competent young people are owed confidentiality; disclosure is for safeguarding or serious harm.
Age alone is not the test; s8 FLRA applies at 16, and Gillick covers under-16s.
Correct: apply Gillick and Fraser, keep confidentiality, consider safeguarding.
The Court of Protection deals with people aged 16 and over who lack capacity, not this situation.
questions.clue: Fifteen years old, understands, cannot be persuaded to tell parents, will continue regardless.
questions.concept: Gillick competence and the Fraser guidelines.

followUp.q: A 17-year-old with capacity consents to an appendicectomy. What is the legal basis for her consent?
followUp.why: Section 8 FLRA 1969 makes the consent of a 16 or 17-year-old to treatment as effective as an adult's. Gillick applies to under-16s, parental consent is not required, and best interests applies only where capacity is lacking.

questions.q: A man with schizophrenia tells his psychiatrist he plans to attack a named neighbour this week. He refuses to let the psychiatrist tell anyone. What does GMC guidance support?
options: Disclose only if a court orders it
Wait until the attack happens and then inform police
Tell his family, because they are next of kin
Disclose the minimum necessary to those who can act to prevent serious harm, telling him first if safe, and record the reasons
questions.why: A credible threat of serious violence to an identifiable person is a classic public-interest justification for disclosure without consent (compare W v Egdell). The disclosure should be proportionate and documented, and the patient told first where it is safe to do so.
optWhy: Confidentiality is not absolute; the public-interest exception exists for exactly this.
Court orders are one legal basis, but the public-interest exception does not need one.
The aim is to prevent serious harm, not report it afterwards.
Next of kin are not the people who can prevent the harm, and telling them is not itself justified.
Correct: proportionate public-interest disclosure.
questions.clue: A credible threat to a named neighbour this week.
questions.concept: Public-interest disclosure to prevent serious harm.

followUp.q: A patient with a newly diagnosed condition that bars driving says he will keep driving his lorry and asks you to keep it confidential. After persuasion fails, what is the next step under GMC guidance?
options: Do nothing, because notification is the driver's legal duty
Tell him you will inform the DVLA, then disclose the relevant information to the DVLA medical adviser and confirm in writing
followUp.why: GMC guidance is to tell the patient you intend to disclose, contact the DVLA medical adviser, and confirm this in writing. The driver's legal duty does not stop the doctor disclosing in the public interest, and the employer or police are not the right recipients.

questions.q: Fifteen-year-old Jade asks her GP for the contraceptive pill and does not want her parents told. Explain the legal framework the GP should apply. (5 marks)
markScheme: Under 16, so s8 FLRA 1969 does not apply; Gillick competence applies (Gillick, House of Lords, 1985)
Assess understanding of nature, purpose, risks and alternatives, and maturity
Fraser guidelines: understands advice; cannot be persuaded to involve parents; likely to have sex anyway; physical or mental health would suffer; best interests
Confidentiality owed to a competent young person; disclosure only for serious harm or safeguarding
Safeguarding: consider exploitation or abuse, age and power imbalance of partner; document; sexual health advice
questions.modelAnswer: Jade is under 16, so s8 Family Law Reform Act 1969 does not apply. She can consent if Gillick competent (House of Lords, 1985), meaning she has enough maturity and understanding of the nature, purpose, risks and alternatives. For contraception the Fraser guidelines apply: she understands the advice; she cannot be persuaded to involve her parents; she is very likely to continue having sex with or without contraception; her physical or mental health is likely to suffer without it; and treatment is in her best interests. A competent young person is owed confidentiality. The GP must still consider safeguarding, such as the partner's age, coercion or exploitation, give sexual health advice, and document the assessment.
questions.concept: Gillick competence and the Fraser guidelines.

questions.q: In the SPIKES framework for breaking bad news, what does the 'K' stand for?
questions.why: K stands for Knowledge: giving the medical information, after a warning shot, in small, jargon-free chunks, checking understanding as you go.
optWhy: Correct: Knowledge, the step of giving the information.
Kindness runs through the whole conversation, but it is not what K stands for.
Checking understanding happens throughout, but it is not the K step.
A key worker may be part of the plan, but that belongs to Strategy and summary.
questions.clue: The letter K in SPIKES.
questions.concept: The steps of breaking bad news.

followUp.q: In SPIKES, which step involves asking how much the patient wants to know?
followUp.why: Invitation asks how much information the patient wants. Setting is preparing the environment; Perception explores what they already know; Emotions is responding with empathy.

questions.q: A patient is given the wrong medication on a ward, causing a short period of drowsiness from which she recovers fully. A staff nurse says it is not serious enough to tell her. What is the correct position?
options: Nothing should be said because no lasting harm occurred
She should be told only if she asks
Only the trust may communicate with her
The professional duty of candour requires telling her what happened, apologising and explaining any effects; the incident should also be reported
An apology should be avoided because it admits liability
questions.why: The professional duty applies whenever something goes wrong with care that causes, or could cause, harm or distress. Each clinician should be open, apologise and explain, and report the incident so that the system learns. Whether the organisation's statutory duty applies depends on the level of harm.
optWhy: The professional duty is not limited to lasting harm.
Candour is proactive; it does not wait for the patient to ask.
Individual clinicians have their own professional duty; the statutory duty adds organisational steps.
Correct: be open, apologise, explain and report.
Under s2 Compensation Act 2006 an apology is not of itself an admission of negligence.
questions.clue: Wrong medication; brief harm; advice not to tell.
questions.concept: Professional duty of candour applies to all errors that cause or could cause harm or distress.

followUp.q: Which statement about the statutory duty of candour (Regulation 20) is correct?
options: It applies to individual doctors rather than organisations
It applies to registered organisations after a notifiable safety incident and requires notification, an apology and written follow-up
It applies only when a patient dies
followUp.why: Regulation 20 applies to CQC-registered providers after notifiable safety incidents (which include moderate and severe harm, not only death) and requires in-person notification, an apology and written follow-up. Individuals have a separate professional duty, which still applies.

questions.q: You are an FY1. Before a theatre list you notice the registrar smells strongly of alcohol and is unsteady. The consultant is in the hospital. What should you do first?
options: Say nothing, because the registrar is senior
Report the registrar to the GMC immediately and leave it to them
Act immediately to protect patients: speak to the registrar if safe and escalate at once to the consultant so the list does not proceed with them operating
Wait until after the list and discuss it at your next supervision
Post an anonymous comment on the trust intranet
questions.why: Patient safety comes first and needs immediate action. Escalating to the consultant who can stop the registrar operating is the fastest effective step; the colleague's health should then be supported through proper channels, with further escalation if the concern is not addressed.
optWhy: Seniority does not remove the duty to act when patients are at risk.
The GMC may be involved later, but it cannot stop today's list; local escalation comes first.
Correct: immediate local action and escalation.
Waiting exposes patients on today's list to risk.
Anonymous comments do not protect today's patients and bypass proper processes.
questions.clue: Alcohol, unsteady, about to operate, consultant available.
questions.concept: Duty to act promptly on patient safety concerns, escalating locally first.

followUp.q: A nurse repeatedly raises concerns about understaffing on a ward and nothing changes after local escalation. What may she do next, with legal protection?
options: Post patient details on social media
Escalate to the trust board or the regulator (CQC), which can be a protected disclosure under the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998
followUp.why: If local routes fail, escalating to senior leadership or a prescribed regulator can be a protected disclosure under PIDA 1998. Sharing patient details publicly breaches confidentiality, and doing nothing or resigning silently leaves patients at risk.

questions.q: A doctor convicted of gross negligence manslaughter was suspended by a medical practitioners tribunal. The GMC appealed and the High Court substituted erasure. On further appeal in 2018, what did the Court of Appeal decide?
options: It upheld erasure because a manslaughter conviction always requires it
It abolished gross negligence manslaughter for doctors
It restored the tribunal's suspension, holding that appeal courts should be slow to interfere with a specialist tribunal's evaluative judgment
questions.why: In Bawa-Garba v GMC the Court of Appeal allowed the doctor's appeal and restored the 12-month suspension. Sanction is an evaluative judgment for the specialist tribunal, which was entitled to weigh systemic failings; there is no presumption that serious harm requires erasure.
optWhy: The Court rejected any automatic link between conviction and erasure.
The conviction was not under appeal in these proceedings.
The offence still exists; only Parliament could abolish it.
No retrial was ordered; the case concerned sanction.
Correct: suspension restored and deference to the tribunal.
questions.clue: Tribunal suspension, High Court erasure, then a 2018 appeal.
questions.concept: Regulatory accountability and the Bawa-Garba appeal.

followUp.q: Which element must be proved for gross negligence manslaughter under R v Adomako?
options: That the breach of duty was so gross as to deserve criminal punishment
That the patient consented to the risk
That the doctor was working alone
followUp.why: Adomako requires a duty, a breach, causation of death and grossness so serious that it deserves criminal punishment. Intention is not required (that would be murder), and consent or working alone are not elements of the offence.

questions.q: Distinguish the statutory duty of candour from the professional duty of candour. (4 marks)
markScheme: Statutory: Regulation 20, Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014
Applies to CQC-registered organisations for notifiable safety incidents: notify in person, apologise, give an account, follow up in writing, keep records
Professional: GMC/NMC duty on each individual clinician
Be open and honest whenever something goes wrong that causes or could cause harm or distress: tell, apologise, offer remedy or support, explain; be open with colleagues, employers and regulators
questions.modelAnswer: The statutory duty of candour is in Regulation 20 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 and is enforced by the CQC. It falls on registered organisations. When a notifiable safety incident occurs, they must tell the person in person as soon as reasonably practicable, apologise, give an account and information, offer support, follow up in writing and keep records. The professional duty, set out jointly by the GMC and NMC, falls on every individual clinician. They must be open and honest with patients whenever something goes wrong with their care that causes, or could cause, harm or distress: tell them, apologise, offer a remedy or support and explain the effects. They must also be open with colleagues, employers and regulators. An apology is not of itself an admission of negligence (s2 Compensation Act 2006).
questions.concept: Organisational versus individual duties of candour.

questions.q: A new blood test for a cancer has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%. A health board proposes using it to screen 10,000 asymptomatic adults in whom the prevalence of the cancer is 1%. (a) Construct the 2×2 table and calculate the PPV and NPV. (b) Recalculate the PPV if the same test were used in a symptomatic clinic population of 10,000 with prevalence 10%. (c) Using your results, advise the board on whether to proceed with population screening, considering both test performance and the UK National Screening Committee criteria. (20 marks)
markScheme: Diseased 100: TP 90, FN 10
Non-diseased 9,900: TN 9,405, FP 495
Explains that PPV depends on prevalence while sensitivity and specificity are unchanged
Harms of false positives (anxiety, invasive follow-up, cost) and of false negatives (missed cases, false reassurance)
Needs RCT evidence that screening reduces mortality or morbidity; survival is biased by lead time, length time and overdiagnosis
Applies UK NSC criteria: condition, test, effective earlier treatment, benefit outweighs harm, value for money, informed choice, capacity for follow-up
Reasoned recommendation, e.g. not yet: use in symptomatic or high-risk groups and support a pilot or RCT
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Of 10,000 people, 100 have the cancer. With 90% sensitivity, TP = 90 and FN = 10. Of the 9,900 without it, 95% specificity gives TN = 9,405 and FP = 495. PPV = 90/(90 + 495) = 90/585 ≈ 15.4%. NPV = 9,405/(9,405 + 10) ≈ 99.9%.

(b) At 10% prevalence: 1,000 have the cancer (TP 900, FN 100) and 9,000 do not (TN 8,550, FP 450). PPV = 900/1,350 ≈ 66.7%. The test is unchanged, but PPV rises sharply because true positives now outnumber false positives.

(c) In the screening population about 85% of positive results are false. Some 495 well people would face anxiety and invasive investigation for every 90 cancers found, and 10 cancers would be missed, with possible false reassurance. Before proceeding, the UK NSC would expect:
- high-quality randomised evidence that screening reduces cancer mortality or morbidity, not just longer survival from diagnosis, which lead-time and length-time bias inflate
- an understanding of the natural history and of how much overdiagnosis occurs
- an effective treatment that works better when started earlier
- benefits that outweigh harms, value for money compared with other uses of the money, and capacity for diagnostic follow-up
- clear information so that people can make an informed choice, plus quality assurance.

Recommendation: do not introduce population screening on these figures alone. The board could use the test as a diagnostic aid in symptomatic or high-risk groups, where the PPV is acceptable, and support a pilot or randomised trial measuring mortality, harms and cost-effectiveness before considering a population programme.
questions.concept: Predictive values depend on prevalence; screening programmes must meet the UK NSC criteria.

questions.q: Mrs Harriet Lowe, 82, has moderate vascular dementia and lives in a care home. She is admitted with a fractured neck of femur. The orthopaedic team recommends hip surgery. Mrs Lowe repeatedly says 'no operations, I want to go home', but cannot recall from one minute to the next that she has broken her hip. Her son, who says he is her 'next of kin', insists she have the surgery. Her daughter says their mother always said she 'never wanted to end up in hospital'. There is no LPA or advance decision on file. Advise the team on how the law in England and Wales governs the decision. (20 marks)
markScheme: Applies MCA 2005 principles: presumption of capacity, all practicable steps to support, unwise decision is not incapacity
Decision-specific and time-specific assessment by the clinician proposing treatment
Functional test first (s3, following JB 2021): unable to retain, and so use or weigh, information about the fracture and options
Causative link (s2): inability caused by dementia (impairment of mind or brain); reasons documented
Support steps: simple explanation, sensory aids, timing, familiar people, repeated attempts
Son as 'next of kin' has no legal power to consent; no LPA, deputy or advance decision
Best interests (s4): past and present wishes, feelings, beliefs and values (daughter's account, current objection), consult family and carers; patient's point of view (Aintree v James 2013)
Weighs clinical factors: surgery offers pain relief and the best chance of mobility and returning home versus anaesthetic risk; consequences of non-operative care
Restraint or confinement only if necessary and proportionate; less restrictive option; deprivation of liberty now judged by the multifactorial test (2026)
Disputes: best-interests meeting, second opinion, mediation or ethics input; Court of Protection if unresolved
questions.modelAnswer:
The Mental Capacity Act 2005 governs this decision.

Capacity. Mrs Lowe is presumed to have capacity (s1). Dementia alone does not prove incapacity, nor does an unwise refusal. The surgeon proposing the operation should assess her capacity for this decision now, after taking all practicable steps to help her: plain language, glasses and hearing aids, a calm setting, her most lucid time of day, familiar carers and repeated attempts.

Following A Local Authority v JB [2021] UKSC 52, the functional question comes first (s3). Can she understand, retain, use or weigh the information (the fracture, the surgery, its risks and benefits, the consequences of refusing) and communicate a decision? Brief retention is enough if she can decide within it, but she cannot hold the fact of the fracture long enough to weigh the options. The team must then establish that this inability is caused by her vascular dementia (s2), and record its reasons.

Who decides. Being 'next of kin' gives her son no power to consent. With no LPA, deputy or advance decision, the treating clinician decides in her best interests.

Best interests (s4). The clinician must weigh her current objection and wish to go home, her long-held views as her daughter reports them, her beliefs and values, and the views of both children and care home staff, trying to see the decision from her point of view (Aintree v James, 2013). Surgery usually offers the best pain relief and the best chance of walking, and so of returning home, which may in fact serve her wish to go home. Non-operative care risks prolonged immobility and complications. These must be balanced against anaesthetic and surgical risk. A best-interests meeting with family, anaesthetist and geriatrician is wise.

Safeguards. Any restraint must be necessary to prevent harm and proportionate, using the less restrictive option. If her care in hospital amounts to a deprivation of liberty, authorisation is needed; since June 2026 this is judged by a multifactorial assessment of her concrete situation, including her expressed wishes, rather than the Cheshire West 'acid test'. If disagreement persists despite second opinions, mediation or ethics input, the trust should apply to the Court of Protection. In a genuine emergency, necessary treatment in her best interests can proceed.
questions.concept: Applying the MCA: capacity, who decides, and best interests.

cases.title: A refusal, a son and a broken hip

steps.text: An 82-year-old woman with moderate vascular dementia is admitted from her care home with a fractured neck of femur. The surgical team recommends an operation. She says repeatedly, 'No operations, I want to go home.' Her son tells the FY1, 'I'm next of kin, so I consent for her.'

ask.q: What is the first legal question the team must answer?
options: Whether she has capacity to make this decision now
Whether the son agrees with surgery
ask.why: Capacity is presumed and decision-specific, so the first step is to assess whether she can make this decision now, after helping her. The son's view matters for best interests but has no legal force; a dementia diagnosis alone does not decide capacity; clinical indication matters but cannot override a capacitous refusal.

steps.text: With glasses and hearing aid in, in a quiet room, she follows a simple explanation and repeats it back, but two minutes later asks why she is in hospital and denies any injury. This happens on three attempts at different times of day.

ask.q: How should this be interpreted under the MCA?
options: She cannot retain the information long enough to use or weigh it, and this appears to be caused by her dementia, so she lacks capacity for this decision
She lacks capacity because she has dementia
She has capacity because she repeated the explanation
Capacity cannot be assessed in dementia
ask.why: Following JB, the functional question comes first: she cannot retain the key facts long enough to weigh them. Only then is the causal link to an impairment of the mind or brain (her dementia) considered. Repeating information immediately is not enough if she cannot hold it to decide; a diagnosis alone never establishes incapacity; and capacity can and must be assessed in dementia.

steps.text: There is no lasting power of attorney or advance decision. Her daughter says their mother always said she never wanted to 'end up in hospital'. The orthopaedic team say surgery gives the best chance of pain control and of walking again.

ask.q: Who makes the decision, and on what basis?
options: The son, as next of kin
The treating clinician, in her best interests, weighing her wishes, values and the family's views
The daughter, because she knows her mother's wishes
ask.why: Without an LPA, deputy or advance decision, the clinician proposing treatment decides in her best interests (s4), weighing her past and present wishes, beliefs and values and consulting family and carers. Neither child has legal authority, and the care home manager has none either.

steps.text: Outcome: at a best-interests meeting the team, both children and a geriatrician agree that surgery offers the best chance of her getting home, which matches her stated wish. She has the operation, with careful pain relief and early mobilisation. Her objection is respected in the way care is delivered, with no restraint, and she returns to her care home three weeks later.

debrief: Assess capacity for the specific decision at the time, after practicable steps to help.
Ask the functional question first, then the causal link to an impairment (JB 2021).
'Next of kin' has no legal power to consent for an adult.
Best interests centres on the patient's own wishes, feelings, beliefs and values, seen from her point of view.
Unresolved disputes go to the Court of Protection.

cases.title: Should I have the test?

steps.text: A 50-year-old man with no symptoms asks his GP about a private blood test advertised as detecting 'early cancer' with 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity. He has no relevant family history.

ask.q: What additional figure is most needed to tell him how likely a positive result is to be correct?
options: The prevalence of the cancer in men like him
The test's sensitivity in a clinic population
The number of laboratories offering it
ask.why: PPV depends on prevalence (pre-test probability) as well as sensitivity and specificity. Sensitivity is already given and does not change with prevalence; price and availability do not affect accuracy.

steps.text: In men like him the prevalence is about 1 in 1,000. The GP builds natural frequencies for 100,000 men: about 100 have the cancer and 90 test positive; of the 99,900 without it, about 4,995 also test positive.

ask.q: About how likely is a positive result to mean he has the cancer?
ask.why: PPV = 90 ÷ (90 + 4,995) ≈ 1.8%, so about 2%. About 90% is the sensitivity, about 95% the specificity, and about 50% would need roughly equal numbers of true and false positives.

steps.text: He asks whether finding cancer earlier 'must be better'. The GP explains lead-time bias, overdiagnosis and the follow-up tests a false positive could lead to, and that there is no randomised evidence that this test reduces deaths.

ask.q: Which principle should guide the rest of the conversation?
options: Persuade him to have the test, because more testing saves lives
Support an informed choice using balanced information on benefits and harms
Tell him the test is illegal
ask.why: UK screening policy and GMC guidance emphasise informed choice with balanced information. Pushing testing ignores harms, refusing to discuss it fails shared decision-making, and the test is not illegal.

steps.text: Outcome: he decides not to buy the test, but takes up his NHS bowel screening invitation, which has trial evidence of benefit. He says the natural-frequency explanation made the trade-off clear.

debrief: PPV depends on prevalence; in low-risk people most positives can be false.
Natural frequencies are easier to understand than percentages.
Longer survival from diagnosis does not prove screening saves lives (lead-time and length-time bias, overdiagnosis).
The aim is informed choice, not maximum uptake.

cases.title: A missed allergy on a night shift

steps.text: At 03:00 an FY1 prescribes a penicillin-class antibiotic for a 70-year-old man with pneumonia. His notes record a penicillin allergy. Twenty minutes after the first dose he develops an itchy rash and mild wheeze.

options: Assess and treat the patient, stop the drug and call for senior help as needed
Amend the drug chart to hide the error
ask.why: Patient safety comes first: assess (ABCDE), stop the antibiotic, treat the reaction and escalate. Reporting and candour follow once he is safe; concealment would be a serious professional failing.

steps.text: He responds to treatment and is well by morning. A nurse says, 'There's no need to make a fuss; he's fine and doesn't know it was a mistake.'

ask.q: What does the professional duty of candour require?
options: Nothing, because there was no lasting harm
Tell him what happened, apologise, explain any effects and make sure the allergy is clearly recorded
Tell him only if he asks
Let the trust decide whether he should ever be told
ask.why: The professional duty applies whenever something goes wrong that causes or could cause harm or distress: be open, apologise, explain and offer support. It is not limited to lasting harm or to patients who ask, and it is a personal duty in addition to any organisational one.

steps.text: The FY1 worries that apologising will be used against them in a claim.

ask.q: Which statement is correct in England and Wales?
options: An apology is an admission of negligence
Only lawyers may apologise to patients
An apology does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence (s2 Compensation Act 2006)
Apologies are banned until an investigation ends
ask.why: Section 2 of the Compensation Act 2006 says an apology or offer of redress does not of itself amount to an admission of negligence. Clinicians are expected to apologise; there is no rule restricting apologies to lawyers or delaying them.

steps.text: Outcome: the FY1 tells the patient and his daughter what happened and apologises. The consultant is informed, an incident report is completed, and the trust adds a prescribing alert. The FY1 reflects on the event with their educational supervisor.

debrief: Treat the patient first, then be open.
The professional duty of candour applies to every clinician, whatever the level of harm.
The statutory duty (Regulation 20) is an additional organisational duty for notifiable safety incidents.
An apology is not of itself an admission of negligence.
Reporting incidents helps the system learn and prevents repeats.

osce.title: Breaking bad news
steps: Prepare: read the notes and results, check the facts, arrange a private room without interruptions (bleep handed over), tissues available
Introduce yourself, confirm the patient's identity, explain the purpose of the conversation and ask whether they would like someone with them
Explore what the patient already knows or suspects about why the tests were done
Ask how much detail they would like to hear now
Give a warning shot (for example, 'I'm afraid the results are not what we had hoped')
Deliver the news clearly in small chunks, without jargon, using the actual word (for example 'cancer') where appropriate
Pause and allow silence; let the patient respond
Acknowledge and respond to emotion with empathy; explore concerns and questions
Check understanding (for example by asking them to tell you in their own words)
Outline the next steps and agree a plan, including who they will see and when
Summarise, offer written information and support contacts, safety-net, and arrange follow-up
Thank the patient and document the conversation
tips: Silence is a skill: resist filling it.
Avoid false reassurance or giving precise prognoses you cannot support.
Use a professional interpreter if needed, never a family member or child.
Check what they want relatives to be told.

osce.title: Assessing capacity for a specific decision
steps: Introduce yourself, confirm identity, explain why you are there and gain agreement to talk
Define the specific decision and the options, including doing nothing, and identify the information relevant to it
Take practicable steps to support the person: right time and place, sensory aids, simple language, visual aids, interpreter or familiar person if helpful
Explain the relevant information, including the reasonably foreseeable consequences of each option and of not deciding
Check understanding by asking the person to explain it back in their own words
Check retention: return to the information after a short interval
Check use or weighing: ask how they are balancing the options and what matters to them
Check communication of a choice by any means
If any ability is lacking, consider whether this is caused by an impairment of, or disturbance in the functioning of, the mind or brain
Consider whether capacity may be regained (for example delirium) and whether the decision can wait
Document the decision, the steps taken, the findings for each ability, the causal link and your conclusion
If capacity is lacking, explain the next steps: best-interests decision, consultation with family and others, any LPA or advance decision
tips: An unwise decision does not by itself show incapacity.
Ask the functional question before the diagnostic one (JB 2021).
Record your reasoning, not just a conclusion.

60–110 (typical adult UK range; varies by lab)

interpret.q: A well 30-year-old with no symptoms has these seven tests as part of an insurance medical. Examination is normal and he drinks little alcohol. Many laboratory reference ranges are set to include the central 95% of results in healthy people. Which is the best interpretation of the ALT?
options: Definite liver disease requiring urgent specialist referral
All the other results must also be abnormal
The laboratory has made an error
The result proves he drinks more than he admits
An isolated, marginal result that may well be normal variation: with seven tests, roughly a 30% chance that at least one falls outside its range by chance; interpret in context and consider repeating
interpret.why: If each range covers 95% of healthy people, about 5% of healthy results fall outside it, so the chance that at least one of seven independent tests is outside its range is 1 − 0.95⁷ ≈ 0.30. A marginal, isolated ALT in a well person should be interpreted in context and usually repeated, rather than treated as proof of disease.
optWhy: A marginal isolated rise in a well person does not establish liver disease or justify urgent referral.
The other six results are within their ranges; one result does not change the others.
Nothing suggests an error; values just outside a range are expected in about 5% of healthy results.
One marginal result cannot prove a particular cause, and the history does not suggest heavy drinking.
Correct: 1 − 0.95⁷ ≈ 30%, so an isolated marginal result is common in healthy people.

interpret.title: New confusion and a decision to make
rows: Usually 96% or above in healthy adults
interpret.q: An 84-year-old woman, usually independent and fully orientated, has a urinary infection and new confusion. These are her observations. She says she does not want to stay in hospital, but cannot follow the explanation of why admission is advised. Which approach best follows the Mental Capacity Act?
options: Accept her refusal, because adults may refuse treatment
Assess capacity now for the urgent decision; if she lacks it, give necessary treatment in her best interests, and reassess when the delirium settles, postponing non-urgent decisions
She has lacked capacity permanently since admission; ask her daughter to decide all future care
Wait until the infection has been treated before doing anything
Discharge her, because confusion means she cannot consent to admission
interpret.why: The observations (fever, tachycardia, fast breathing, lower blood pressure than usual, new confusion) suggest acute illness with delirium, which can temporarily impair capacity. Capacity is time-specific: assess it for the urgent decision now, act in her best interests if she lacks capacity, and consider whether she may regain capacity, deferring decisions that can wait.
optWhy: A refusal is binding only if she has capacity; she cannot follow the explanation, so capacity must be assessed first.
Correct: assess now for the urgent decision, act in best interests, and reassess as she recovers.
Capacity is time-specific and delirium may resolve; her daughter has no authority without an LPA.
Her observations suggest she may be acutely unwell, so delaying necessary treatment could cause serious harm.
Lack of capacity does not justify abandoning treatment; it triggers a best-interests decision.
